words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today we are learning our maths words. These are the special words we use when we count. Words like count, how many, and more. Why? Because when you know the words, you understand the question. Then maths feels easy. Here is what I expect from you. Listen to each word. Then tell me the word back in your own way. That is all! You will need something to count. Buttons, beans, or small stones. Or just your fingers! We will do three words together. Let's start with something small. Word one: count. To count means you say the number names while you touch each thing. One touch, one number. Try it now. Hold up your fingers and count them slowly: one, two, three, four, five. Did you touch each finger as you said the number? Tell me when you have done it. 😊

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Unit 1: Numbers to 10. In this lesson you will learn to count things one by one, read and write the numbers 0 to 10, and say which group has more. We do this because counting is the very first tool in maths — everything later stands on it. Please get a little pile of small things: beans, buttons, stones or bottle caps. About 20. Also a pencil and paper. Here is what I expect from you: touch each object as you count, say the numbers out loud, and tell me your answer even if you are not sure. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Put 5 objects in a straight line on the table. Touch each one with your finger as you say: one, two, three, four, five. Then tell me: how many objects altogether?

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. 😊

This page is our Unit Overview for Unit 1, Numbers to 10. An overview is a quick look at everything we will learn. We do it so you know where we are going, and so you can get your things ready. By the end of this unit you will count things up to 10, read and write the numbers 0 to 10, and say which group has more. There are 4 small steps. I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Go and find some small things you can count. Dates, beans, stones, bottle caps or buttons all work well. You need about 20 of them. Put them in a little pile next to you. You can ask your grown-up to help you find them. Tell me when you have your pile ready.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Hello! Today we are on Explore the Concept. That means we look at numbers to 10 and try them out ourselves. We do this so counting stops being just words, and starts meaning real things you can touch. Here is what I expect from you: touch each thing once, count out loud, and tell me your answer. Guessing fast is fine to try, but always check by counting. You will need a pencil and, if you can, a few small things like beans, stones or bottle caps. There are 6 short steps. Step 1. Count these dates. Touch each one on your screen as you say the number. 🌴🌴🌴🌴🌴

How many dates are there altogether?

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Learn the Method. A method is just a way of doing something, step by step. Our first method is Counting Objects One by One. We do this so your counting is always right, never rushed. By the end, you will be able to count up to 10 things and say how many altogether. You will need a few small things you can touch — dates, beans, stones, buttons, or even your fingers. There are 3 steps, and I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Put 7 of your small things in a row on the table. Make a straight line, and do not let them touch or sit on top of each other. I am looking for a neat row where I could see every single one. Tell me when your row is ready. 🙂

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today we are working with Visual Models. A visual model is a picture that helps you SEE a number, not just say it. We do this because numbers are easier when you can see them and touch them. By the end, you will be able to count things, show a number on a ten-frame, and say which group has more. There are 5 steps. Please get a little pile of small things — beans, stones, buttons or bottle caps. About 20 of them. Also a pencil and paper. Here comes step 1: counting real objects. Put 5 of your things in a straight line. Touch each one as you say: one, two, three, four, five. Then tell me: how many are there altogether? I am looking for one touch for each thing, and the last number as your answer.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Worked Examples. A worked example is a maths problem with the answer already worked out, step by step. We look at them together so you can see HOW a good mathematician thinks. By the end, you will be able to count a group and say how many altogether, all by yourself. You need two things: your eyes and your pointing finger. If you have some small things nearby, like beans, buttons or stones, keep them close too. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Look at this group of dates. 🔴🔴🔴🔴🔴🔴🔴

Point at each red date with your finger and say the numbers out loud: one, two, three... Touch each one only once. What I expect from you: tell me the LAST number you said.

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Welcome! Today we are doing our "Practise together" activity. You will pick one idea from Unit 1, make it with real things or a drawing, and show it to someone at home. We do this because numbers feel easy when you can touch them and talk about them. There are 4 steps. Get a pencil, some paper, and a few small things you can count — beans, buttons, stones, or bottle caps. A grown-up can help you find them. Step 1: choose ONE idea from our unit to practise. You can pick:
counting things one at a time,
a ten-frame,
writing the numbers 0 to 10,
or comparing two groups (more and fewer). Tell me which one you choose. 🙂

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text:
Hello! Today we are doing Guided Practice for Numbers to 10. This is where you count things and find missing numbers, with me helping you at each step. We do it so your counting gets slow, careful and correct — that is what good mathematicians do. By the end, you will be able to count up to 10 things without skipping any, and fill in a missing number in a number track. You need one thing: your finger, to touch each picture as you count. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Count these bottle caps. Touch each one on the screen as you say the number out loud. 🔵🔵🔵🔵🔵🔵

Tell me how many bottle caps there are. A good answer is one number, said after touching every cap once.

games.label: Games
games.text:
Welcome to our Games page! These games are quick number challenges about counting to 10. We play them so counting becomes fast and easy for you, like knowing your own name. By the end, you will be able to count a group of things and say the total without getting muddled. You need two things: your eyes for careful looking, and one finger for touching each thing as you count. Take your time — there's no rush. There are 4 rounds in our first game, "Quick Match: Count". I will give you one round at a time, and you type your answer to me. Here comes question one. Count the buttons: 🔘🔘🔘🔘🔘🔘🔘

How many buttons are there? Touch each one on the screen as you count, and tell me the last number you say.

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Math Fluency. Fluency means being quick and sure with numbers. In this activity you count things, say numbers in order, and find missing numbers. By the end you will count up to 10 without stopping to think hard. You need your eyes, your finger for touching and counting, and maybe a pencil. Here is what I expect from you: touch each thing once as you count, say the last number as your answer, and tell me how you got it. Guessing is fine to start, but I will always ask "how did you know?"

There are 3 rounds, with 4 questions in each round. Round 1, here comes question one. Count the buttons. Touch each one as you count. 🔘🔘🔘🔘🔘🔘🔘

How many buttons?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. 😊

This page is called Solve Real Problems. It gives you little counting problems from real life, like counting moons in the sky or bread at the market. We do it so your counting works everywhere, not just on paper. By the end, you will count carefully and say how many altogether. All you need is your finger to touch each picture, and your voice to count out loud. Here is what I expect from you: touch each thing once, count slowly out loud, then tell me the last number you said. Take your time — there's no rush. There are 6 problems. Here comes question one. ★ 🌙 🌙 → how many moons? Careful — the star is just a marker. We only count moons. Tell me your answer.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today we are doing Explain Your Thinking. 🌟

This is where you tell me HOW you worked something out, not just the answer. We do it because a real mathematician can say why their answer is right. By the end, you will be able to talk through your counting out loud. You will need a few small things to count — dates, beans, stones or buttons — and a grown-up nearby if you want one. What I expect from you: a full answer in your own words, using words like count, how many, and altogether. Short is fine. Talking it out loud first is allowed! There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Get 6 small things and put them in a line in front of you. Tell me when your line of 6 is ready. Take your time — there's no rush.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Welcome to your Unit Challenge! 🌟

This is where you show off everything you learned about numbers to 10. You will make your own model, explain it out loud, and even write your very own maths question. Get these ready: paper, a pencil, and about 10 small things to count. Beans, buttons, stones or bottle caps all work well. There are 4 steps. I will give you one step at a time, and I will wait for you each time. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Choose one idea from this unit. Here are your choices:
Counting things one at a time
A ten-frame (the 2 rows of 5 cups)
Comparing two groups: more and fewer
Numbers in order from 0 to 10

What I expect from you: pick just ONE and tell me which one. Any of them is a good choice — pick the one you like best. Which one do you choose?

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and our lesson is all about shapes. 🟦

This lesson is called Geometry. We will meet solid shapes you can hold — a ball, a tin, a box — and flat shapes you can draw, like circles and squares. We do this because shapes are everywhere in your home, and naming them helps you talk about the world like a mathematician. Here is what I expect from you: hold real things in your hands, count out loud, and tell me your answer each time. Guessing is fine! Mistakes are how we learn. You will need three things from your kitchen or toy box, and a grown-up can help you find them. There are 5 steps in our lesson. Step 1: Go and find these three things — a ball (or an orange), a tin can (or a cup), and a box (or a die from a game). Put them on the table in front of you. Tell me when you have them, and tell me what you found. 🙂

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Welcome! This page is our Maths Words page. It holds the special shape words for this unit, like cube, sphere and face. We do this so the words feel easy in your mouth. Then when a question says "how many faces?", you will know just what it means. Here is what I expect from you: say each word out loud, tell me the meaning in your own words, and find one real thing in your room that matches. Your own words are perfect — they do not have to sound like a book. There are 4 steps. You just need your voice and your eyes. Ready? Here comes step 1. Step 1: Our first word is sphere. A sphere is a shape that is round all over, with no flat parts — like a ball. Say "sphere" out loud. Then look around you and tell me one thing that is a sphere. 🙂

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Unit Overview. This is where we look at what Unit 2 is all about: shapes. By the end of this unit, you will name solid shapes like the ball and the box, and flat shapes like the circle and the square. Today we just take a first look, so nothing is hard. You will need your eyes, your hands, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. There are 4 small steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Look around the room and find something round like a ball. It could be a real ball, an orange, or anything round all over. Hold it in your hand. Then tell me what you found.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Hello! Today we are shape detectives. 🕵️

This activity is called Explore the Concept. You will hold real things from your home and find out what shape they are. We do this because shapes are easier to learn with your hands than with your eyes. By the end, you will name a sphere, a cube and a cylinder, and know which ones roll. You will need three things: a ball, a box, and a tin can. You can ask your grown-up to help you find them. There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Go and get your ball and your box. Hold one in each hand. Feel them all over with your fingers. Then tell me: which one is round all over, with no flat parts?

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Shape Models activity. On this page we look at models of shapes — pictures and real things that help us SEE what a shape is. We do it because shapes are much easier to learn when you hold them and look at them, not just read about them. By the end, you will be able to name a cube, a sphere and a cylinder, and say which ones roll and which ones stack. You will need three things from your home: a ball, a tin can (or a cup), and a box. You can ask your grown-up to help you find them. Here is what I expect from you: try each step out loud, and tell me what you see. Wrong answers are fine — mistakes are how we learn. We have 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Go and find your three things — a ball, a tin can, and a box. Put them in front of you on the table. Tell me when you have them. 😊

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Learn the Method". 🙂

A method is just a way of doing something, step by step. Our method today is "Naming 3D Shapes by Touch". By the end, you will hold three real things and name them: sphere, cylinder, cube. Here is what I expect from you: pick up each object with your hands, say the name out loud, and tell me your answer in the chat. A grown-up can help you find the objects. There are 3 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Go and find three things. A ball. A tin can or a tube. A box or a die. Put all three in front of you. Tell me when you have them. 👍

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today we are on the Worked Examples page. A worked example is a maths problem with the answer shown, step by step, like watching me solve it first. We do this so you can see how a good answer sounds. Then you can do one yourself. By the end you will be able to name shapes like sphere, cube and cylinder, and count sides. You need: your eyes, your voice, and if you can, a ball, a tin can and a box from home. Ask your grown-up to help you find them. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Hold or think about a ball. Tell me two things — is it round all over, or does it have flat parts? And what is its shape name? A good answer sounds like this: "It is round all over, so it is a ..." You finish it! 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text:
Welcome to Guided Practice! 🌟

Here is what this is. I will give you shape questions, one at a time. You look, think, and tell me your answer. This is how we make our shape learning strong. By the end, you will be able to name shapes and count their sides all by yourself. What you need: your eyes, your thinking, and maybe one real object to hold. Take your time — there's no rush. There are 12 short questions. I will give you one, then wait for you. Here comes question one. Look at an orange, or picture one in your head. Is it a sphere, a cube, or a cylinder?

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today we are doing our "Practise together" activity for Geometry. You will pick one shape idea from this unit, then make or draw a model of it, show it to someone at home, and make up your own shape question. We do this because making and telling something is the best way to make it stick in your head. You will need paper, a pencil, and some things from home like a ball, a box, or a tin. There are 4 steps. I will give you one at a time, and I will wait for you each time. Step 1: Choose ONE idea from our unit to practise. You could choose 3D shapes (cube, sphere, cylinder), or shapes that roll and stack, or flat 2D shapes and their sides. Tell me which one you choose, and say one thing you already know about it. 😊

games.label: Games
games.text: Welcome to our Games page! These are quick shape games. Each game has four little questions about shapes like the cube, the sphere and the cylinder. We play them because games help your brain remember shapes fast, without it feeling like work. By the end you will name shapes and say how many sides they have, quickly and surely. Here is what I expect from you: answer with the shape name or the number, and then tell me how you knew. Guessing is okay, but thinking out loud is better! You need nothing but your eyes, your fingers for counting, and your voice. There are four questions in our first game. Here comes question one. Which 3D shape is round all over and rolls in every direction? Is it a sphere, a cube, a rectangle, or a triangle?

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Math Fluency. Math Fluency means quick shape questions. I ask, you answer fast — like a game. We do it so shape names pop into your head without thinking hard. By the end you will name shapes quickly and say which ones roll and which ones stack. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a ball and a box nearby to touch. There are 3 rounds. I will give you one question at a time. I expect you to try an answer even if you are not sure — a guess with thinking is good, and "I don't know" is fine too. Here comes question one. Name the 3D shape of a football. Is it round all over, or does it have flat parts?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Welcome to Solve Real Problems! 🌟

In this activity we find shapes in real life — at home, at the market, on a trip. We do it because shapes are everywhere, not just on paper. By the end, you will name shapes and count their sides like a shape detective. You need your eyes, and a pencil if you like. There are 6 little problems. I will give you one at a time. Here comes question one. Look at a box, like a box of dates or a shoe box. 📦
What is the name of this 3D shape? I am hoping to hear a shape name, and if you can, one reason why. Take your time — there's no rush.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Welcome to Explain Your Thinking! This is where you say your maths out loud, in your own words. We do it because knowing an answer is good, but explaining WHY is even better. By the end, you will be able to tell someone why shapes roll or stay still. You need your voice, and if you can, a ball and a box near you. There are 3 short questions, one at a time. Here comes question one. Explain why a sphere rolls but a cube does not. A good answer talks about the ball being round all over, and the box having flat parts. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me what you think! 🙂

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Hello! Today we are doing the Unit Challenge for our shapes unit. 🌟

Here is what it is. You will pick one shape idea you liked, make it with things at home or draw it, tell a grown-up about it, and then make up one shape question of your own. We do this because saying a shape out loud, in your own words, is the best way to show you really know it. Here is what I expect from you: use real shape words like cube, sphere, cylinder, circle, square, triangle, sides and corners. Take your time — there's no rush. You will need paper, a pencil, and a few things from your home like a ball, a tin, or a box. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Choose ONE idea from this unit. For example, "shapes that roll and shapes that stack", or "counting sides and corners". Tell me which idea you choose. 😊

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and our lesson is all about halves. A half means one of two equal parts of a whole. By the end you will be able to make halves, spot them, and know that two halves make one whole. You will need a few paper shapes (a circle, a square, a rectangle), a pencil, and a grown-up nearby if you use scissors. There are 5 steps. I will give you one step at a time, and I will wait for you each time. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Find one whole thing. Pick up one paper shape, or one biscuit, or one piece of fruit. Hold it up and say out loud: "This is the whole."

What I expect from you: tell me what your whole thing is. Just one thing, complete, not broken yet. What is your whole?

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Welcome to Unit 3! I'm your teacher today, and our unit is called Fractions: Halves. 🙂

This page is the Unit Overview. It is like looking at a map before we start a trip. We look at what we will learn, and we get our things ready. By the end of today's walk-through, you will know what a whole is, what a half is, and you will have your paper shapes ready to fold. Here is what I expect from you: talk to me after each step, even one or two words is fine. There are 4 steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Get your things ready. You need some scrap paper, a pencil or crayon, and safety scissors. Ask your grown-up to help you cut out one paper circle and one paper square. Tell me when you have your paper shapes.

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Math Words & Symbols page. This page has the special maths words for Unit 3, all about halves. We learn them so that when I say "equal" or "whole", you know exactly what I mean. By the end, you will be able to say each word and tell me what it means in your own words. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: the word whole. Whole means the complete thing, before it is split. A whole biscuit. A whole mango. Nothing taken away. Now you try. Tell me one whole thing you can see near you right now. Something complete, not broken.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Explore the Concept. In this activity we look at halves. A half is one of two equal parts of a whole. We do it so you can see halves in real things, like biscuits and paper shapes. By the end, you will be able to spot a half and say why it is a half. You need a pencil, a piece of paper, and your thinking brain. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are six little steps. I will give you one at a time. Step 1. Picture a whole biscuit in your mind. Now you break it into two pieces. Before you broke it, what do we call the complete biscuit? I am looking for one word. Take your time — there's no rush. 🙂

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Visual Models. A visual model is just a picture that shows a maths idea. On this page we look at pictures of shapes to learn about halves. We do it because halves are much easier to see than to hear about. By the end, you will be able to look at any shape and say, "Yes, those are halves!" or "No, they are not."

You will need a pencil, some scrap paper, and your eyes ready to look carefully. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Look at the first picture on your screen, called A Whole and Its Parts. Now pick up one piece of scrap paper. That whole piece of paper is called the whole. Tear it into two pieces. Tell me: how many parts do you have now?

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! Let's look at this page together. This page is called Learn the Method. A method is just a set of steps — a recipe for doing something in maths. Today's method shows that a half is one of two equal parts of a whole. We do this so you can share things fairly, like a biscuit or a chapati with your brother or sister. What I expect from you: try each step yourself, then tell me what happened. Short answers are perfect. If you get stuck, just say "stuck" and I will help. You will need one piece of paper and a pencil. You can ask your grown-up to help you. There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Hold up your piece of paper. Say out loud: "This is the whole paper."

Then tell me — what does the word whole mean? 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today we are doing Guided Practice for halves. That means I give you one question at a time, and you tell me your answer. We do this so the big idea sticks: a half is one of two equal parts of a whole. Equal means the same size. By the end you will be able to spot halves, and make halves yourself. You will need a pencil, some scrap paper, and a grown-up nearby if you want to cut or fold. Take your time — there's no rush. There are 12 questions. We start easy and get a little harder. Here comes question one. Kaltun has one whole mango. She cuts it into two equal pieces. What do we call each piece?

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Worked Examples page. Worked examples are stories where someone solves a halves problem, one step at a time. We read them so you can copy the thinking later, all by yourself. By the end you will know what a half is, and how to check it is fair. You need your eyes, your brain, and a pencil and paper if you have one. There are 4 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1. Here is our first story. Amina has one whole date. She wants to share it fairly with her little brother. I expect one short answer from you: how many pieces should Amina make, and should they be the same size or different sizes?

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today we are doing our Practise together activity. Here is what it is: you will pick one idea about halves, make it with paper, show it to someone at home, and then make up your own halves question. We do this because when you build a half with your own hands, you really understand it — not just remember it. You will need paper, a pencil, and a grown-up nearby to help with folding or cutting. I expect you to try each step yourself, and tell me what you made. Wobbly lines are fine! Careful thinking is what counts. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Choose one idea from our unit to show. You could choose "two equal parts make halves", or "two halves make a whole", or "a shape can be halved in more than one way". Which one would you like to show? 😊

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Math Fluency. Math Fluency means quick practice. I ask a short question about halves, and you answer in your own words. It helps the ideas become fast and easy in your head. By the end, you will be able to say what a half is and spot when parts are equal. You need just your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. We will do Round 1 together. That is four questions, one at a time. I do not need perfect words — I want you to tell me what you think and why. Take your time. There's no rush. Here comes question one. One whole biscuit is broken into two equal pieces. What is each piece called?

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Games page for Unit 3: Halves. These games are little quick quizzes. Each game has four questions about halves. We play them so your brain gets fast at spotting when two parts are equal — that is what makes a half. What I expect from you: pick your answer yourself first, then tell me. Say the whole answer out loud or type it. It is okay to be wrong — mistakes are how we learn. There are 4 rounds in our first game. Here comes step one. Step 1: Open the game called "Quick Match: Whole". Read the first question on your screen. It asks: which of these describes a half? Look at all four choices before you pick. Then tell me which one you chose.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello! This page is called Solve Real Problems. Here we use halves in real life — sharing food at home, at the market, on a journey. We do this because halves are not just on paper. You use them every day when you share fairly with someone. By the end, you will be able to look at two pieces and say "yes, that is a half" or "no, that is not fair."

You just need your thinking brain, and maybe a pencil to draw. There are 6 problems, and we will do one at a time. Here comes question one. Maryan has one whole chapati for breakfast. She wants to share it fairly with her little brother, so they each get a half. How should she cut it? Tell me in your own words. I am listening. 🙂

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Welcome to Explain Your Thinking! On this page you look at a shape, then tell me WHY in your own words. We do this because a good mathematician can say how they know, not just point. By the end, you will be able to say what makes two parts halves, using the words whole, half, and equal. You need your voice and your thinking. A pencil and paper shape nearby will help too. There are 3 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: A square is cut into one big part and one small part. Tell me why this is NOT halves. A good answer uses the word equal. Take your time — there's no rush.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Welcome to your Unit Challenge! 🌟

This is where you show what you know about halves. You will make your own model of a half, explain it to someone at home, and then make up your own halves question. By the end, you will be able to show and say what a half is all by yourself. You will need paper, a pencil, and maybe a small snack or paper shape you can fold. There are 4 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Choose one big idea from this unit to show. You could choose "a half is two equal parts", or "two halves make a whole", or "halves can be different shapes". Tell me which idea you pick, and I'll help you build it.

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text:
Welcome! This page is our Maths Words page for Unit 4. These are the special words we use to talk about size. Learning them means you can say exactly what you see, like "the tree is taller than the bush."

By the end, you will know three big words and use each one in your own sentence. You just need your voice, and maybe your eyes to look around the room. There are 4 steps. Step 1: Our first word is tall. Tall means how far something goes from the bottom to the top, standing up. Look around you right now. Can you tell me one thing you see that is tall?

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today's lesson is called Measures. That means comparing sizes of things. We will learn words like taller, shorter, longer and wider. By the end, you will be able to look at two things and say which one is bigger, and even measure with blocks. You will need a pencil, some blocks or bottle caps, and a few things from around you — like a spoon, a cup, a pencil. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one! Step 1: Tall and short. Height is how far it is from the bottom to the top. Find two cups, or two toys. Stand them both on the same table, side by side. Now tell me: which one is taller? Try to say it in a full sentence, like "The big cup is taller than the small cup."

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today we start Unit 4. It is called Measures. Measures means comparing sizes. We will say which thing is taller and which is shorter. We will say which is longer, and which is wider. At the end, you will even measure things by counting blocks! What I expect from you: say your answers in a full sentence, like "the cup is taller than the spoon." Full sentences help the words stick. You will need your eyes, your voice, and two things from near you. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Find two things near you that are different heights. Maybe a cup and a spoon, or a bottle and a toy. Stand them both on the same table. Then tell me which one is taller.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Hello! Today we are doing "Explore the Concept" in Unit 4: Measures. In this activity, we look at two things and say which one is bigger — taller, longer, or wider. We do it so you can talk about size with the right words, like a real mathematician. By the end, you will be able to say full sentences like "the date palm is taller than the bush."

You will need your eyes, your voice, and one finger for pointing. If you have two cups near you, grab them — but pictures in your head work too! Here is what I expect from you: not just one word. I want the whole sentence, with the word "than" in it. Take your time — there's no rush. There are 6 little steps. Here comes step one. A tall cup and a short cup stand side by side on the same table. Their bottoms both touch the table. Which cup is taller? Tell me in a full sentence. 😊

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Learn the Method."

A method is just a set of steps we follow to do something well. In this unit we learn how to compare sizes. We start with height — how far it is from the bottom to the top. By the end, you will be able to look at two things and say which one is taller and which one is shorter, in a full sentence. What you need: two things from around you that stand up. A tall cup and a short cup are perfect. A bottle and a mug also work. Ask your grown-up if you need help finding them. This method has 3 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Put your two objects side by side on the same flat table or floor. Their bottoms must both touch the table — no one standing on a book! I expect you to tell me the two things you chose. 😊

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models page in Unit 4, Measures. Visual models are pictures that show us size ideas. We will look at five of them, one at a time. By the end, you will be able to say which thing is taller, longer or wider, and count how many blocks tall something is. You need your eyes, your finger for pointing, and your voice. If you have some blocks or bottle caps nearby, keep them close for later. There are five steps, one for each model. Here comes step one. Step 1: Comparing Height. On your page, find the first model with two things standing side by side. Put your finger at the bottom of one, and slide it up to the top. Then do the same on the other one. I expect you to tell me one full sentence, like this: "The ___ is taller than the ___."

Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me your sentence when you are ready.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Guided Practice in Measures. 📏

In this activity we compare things by size. We say which one is taller, which one is longer, and which one is wider. We do this so you can use the right word for the right kind of size. By the end, you will be able to say a full sentence like "the date palm is taller than the bush."

You need your voice and your thinking brain. A pencil and paper are nice, but not needed. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. A tall cup and a short cup stand side by side on the same table. Which cup is taller? Try to answer in a full sentence, like this: "The ___ cup is taller than the ___ cup."

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today we are doing the "Practise together" activity for our Measures unit. This activity is where you show what you know about size — tall and short, long and short, wide and thin. You will draw or build something, then explain it out loud to someone in your family. By the end, you will be able to say a full sentence like "the spoon is longer than the crayon" all by yourself. That is the big goal. You will need paper, a pencil, and a few things from around your home — like a spoon, a cup, a shoe, or a toy. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one! Step 1: Pick ONE idea from our unit to practise. You can choose taller and shorter, or longer and shorter, or wider and thinner. Just tell me which one you pick. There is no wrong choice! 😊

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Worked Examples page. 📏

A worked example is a maths puzzle with the thinking shown. We read the puzzle, we think first, then we check the thinking together. We do this so you learn the words taller, longer and wider — and so you learn to say WHY. Here is what I expect from you: try to answer before you look at the solution, and always say a full sentence, like "the cup is taller than the bowl."

We have 4 steps. Ready? Here comes step one. Step 1. Look at the first worked example: a tall date palm tree and a small bush. The tree reaches high into the sky. The bush only reaches your knee. Tell me in a full sentence: which one is taller?

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Math Fluency. Math Fluency means quick practice questions about size. You will say which thing is taller, longer, or wider. This helps the size words feel easy and fast in your head. Here is what I expect from you: answer in a full sentence, like "the tree is taller than the stool". And take your time — there's no rush. We have three rounds, with a few questions in each. Let's start with something small. Here comes question one. A date palm tree and a small stool stand side by side. Which one is taller?

games.label: Games
games.text:
Welcome to our Games page! 🎉

Here you will play short games about size words: taller, shorter, longer, wider and thinner. We play them so the words become quick and easy in your head. By the end, you will be able to look at two things and say which is taller, longer or wider — in a full sentence. You need: your eyes, your voice, and your finger to tap the answers. Here is what I expect from you: choose one answer, then tell me WHY you chose it. The "why" is the real learning. There are 3 steps in our game time today. Step 1: Look at your screen and find the first game. It is called Quick Match: Tall / taller than. Tap it to open it. Tell me when it is open. 😊

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today we are doing Solve Real Problems. This is where we use our measuring words in real life — at home, at the market, and on a trip. We do this so the words stick when you see real things, not just pictures. By the end, you will be able to say which thing is longer, shorter, or wider, and tell me HOW you know. What you need: your voice, and your eyes to picture each thing. A pencil and paper if you like. There are 6 problems. What I expect from you each time: give me your answer in a full sentence, like "the snake is longer than the worm." Then tell me one reason. Here comes question one. A snake and a worm. Which one is longer?

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Welcome to Explain Your Thinking! In this activity you tell me an answer AND how you know it. We do this because a good mathematician can say why, not just what. By the end, you will be able to say a full sentence like "the snake is longer than the worm, and I know because..."

You just need your voice and your thinking brain. There are 3 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1. Here is the question: a mouse and an elephant. Is the mouse taller or shorter? Tell me your word, and then tell me how you know. 🐭🐘

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Hello! Today's activity is our Unit Challenge. It is called "Practise together."

In it, you pick one big idea from Unit 4 — like taller and shorter, longer and shorter, or wider and thinner — and you show it with real things or a drawing. We do this because saying an idea out loud, in your own words, is how it really sticks in your head. By the end you will be able to compare two things and say a full sentence like "the spoon is longer than the crayon."

You will need paper, a pencil, and a few things from around your home. A grown-up nearby can help you. There are four steps. Here is step one. Step 1: Choose ONE idea from this unit to show. You can pick tall and short, long and short, or wide and thin. I am hoping you just tell me which one you picked, and why you like it. Which one will it be? 😊

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Unit Overview. This page is like a map of Unit 5. It shows what we will learn: adding, taking away, and writing number sentences like 3 + 2 = 5. We look at the map first so you know where we are going. What I expect from you: talk to me in short answers, try each little task, and it is fine to be wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. You will need a pencil and about 10 small things you can count — stones, buttons, dried beans or bottle caps. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Go and get your 10 small counting things. Put them on the table in front of you. Then tell me what you chose. 🙂

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this lesson is called Working with Numbers to 10. In this lesson we learn to put groups together (add) and take some away (subtract). We do it because adding and taking away are things we use every day, like counting snacks or toys. By the end, you will be able to say and write things like 3 + 2 = 5. You will need a grown-up nearby and 10 small things you can hold — stones, buttons, dried beans or bottle caps all work. What I expect from you is this: touch the objects, count out loud, and tell me your answer each time. Take your time — there's no rush. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Put 3 of your objects in one small group. Then put 2 more in a second group beside it. Count each group out loud so you know they are right. When both groups are ready, tell me "done".

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for our Maths Words page. This page has the special maths words we use in Unit 5, like add, equals and take away. We learn them so that when a question says "altogether" or "take away", you know exactly what to do. By the end, you will be able to say what each word means in your own words. You need a pencil, some paper, and about 10 small things you can count — stones, buttons or dried beans are perfect. There are 4 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Get your counting things ready, and put 3 of them in one little pile and 2 in another little pile on the table. When they are ready, tell me "done".

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! I'm your teacher today, and this page is called Explore the Concept. Here we play with real things to find out how adding and taking away work. By the end you will be able to put two groups together and say how many altogether. You need about 10 small things you can hold — buttons, stones, beans, or bits of pasta. Ask your grown-up if you need help finding them. There are six little discoveries. Here comes discovery one. Put 3 of your objects in one group. Then put 2 more in a different group beside it. Now push the two groups together and count them all. I expect you to touch each object once as you count, and then tell me the total. Take your time — there's no rush. How many are there altogether?

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models page. 😊

A visual model is a picture that helps you SEE the maths, not just say it. On this page there are six models, like six little pictures of adding and taking away. By the end you will be able to show a sum with real objects and say it out loud. You need six small things you can move: stones, beans, buttons or bottle caps. Ask your grown-up to help you find them. We have six steps, one model each. Here comes step one! Step 1: Addition as Combining. Put 3 of your stones in one small group. Put 2 stones in another group. I expect you to count each group out loud, then push them together and count them all. Tell me: how many stones are there altogether?

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Learn the Method". A method is just a way of doing something, step by step. Today's method is Counting Two Groups Altogether. By the end, you will be able to put two groups together and say how many there are altogether. You will need about 10 small things — buttons, stones, dried beans, or bits of pasta. Ask your grown-up if you need help finding them. There are 3 steps, and I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Put 4 of your things in one little group on the table. Count them out loud, touching each one: one, two, three, four. I expect you to touch each thing once as you say the number. That is what good counting looks like! Tell me when your first group is ready. 😊

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is Worked Examples. A worked example is a maths problem with every step shown, so you can see HOW to think, not just the answer. We do these so that when you meet a new sum on your own, you know what to do first. By the end you will be able to add two groups, add 1 more, and take some away — and write it as a number sentence. You will need a pencil, some paper, and about 10 small things you can move — stones, buttons, beans or bottle caps. We have 4 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Get your things ready. Put your 10 small counters in front of you, and your pencil and paper beside them. What I expect: your counters in one little pile, and paper ready to write on. Tell me when you are ready. 😊

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today we are doing the "Practise together" activity. In this activity you pick one idea from Unit 5, like adding, taking away, or number bonds. You make it real with things you can hold, like stones, buttons or dates. Doing maths with your hands helps the idea stick in your head. By the end, you will be able to show and explain an addition or a take away all by yourself. You will need paper, a pencil, and some small objects you can count. There are 4 steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Choose one idea from this unit. You could pick adding two groups together, or taking away, or number bonds that make 10. Tell me which idea you choose. 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today we are doing Guided Practice for Unit 5. Guided Practice means we work through maths questions together, one at a time. We will add groups together, and take some away. By the end, you will be able to add and take away numbers up to 10, and say your answer out loud. You will need a pencil and paper, and 10 small things you can hold — dates, stones, buttons or bottle caps all work well. Ask your grown-up to help you find them. Here is what I expect from you: try each one yourself first, then tell me your answer AND how you got it. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 6 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1. Put 2 dates in front of you. Now put 1 more date next to them. Count them all. How many dates altogether? 🙂

games.label: Games
games.text: Welcome to the Games page! These games are short and quick. Each game gives you four questions about adding and taking away. You pick the right answer, and you try to get at least 3 right. We play these to make our adding and taking away fast — like practising kicking a ball again and again. Here is what I expect from you: think first, then tell me your answer. And tell me HOW you worked it out. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. You need your fingers, or 10 small things like stones, buttons or dried beans. Go and get them if you can. There are 4 steps. Step 1: Get your 10 small counting things and put them in front of you. Then say "ready" to me. 😊

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Welcome! Today we are doing Solve Real Problems. These are little story problems about real life — dates from Mum and Dad, beads at the market, goats on the road. You work out the maths hiding inside the story. By the end, you will be able to hear a story and turn it into an adding sentence like 4 + 3 = 7. You will need a pencil and paper, and some small things to count — stones, beans or buttons are perfect. Your fingers work too! What I expect from you: tell me your answer AND how you got it. In maths, the thinking is the best part. 😊

There are 6 problems. Here comes question one. At home, Amina's mother gives her 4 dates. Her father gives her 3 more dates. How many dates does Amina have altogether? Take your time — there's no rush.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Today we are doing Explain Your Thinking. That means you tell me the maths in your own words, not just the answer. 🙂

We do this because saying "why" out loud shows you really understand it — and it makes the idea stick. What I expect from you: use full sentences, use our maths words like add, altogether and equals, and always tell me why. You will need your voice and maybe a few small things to count — stones, beans or buttons. There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Step one: think about this question, but do not answer yet. What does "altogether" mean when we put two groups together? Just tell me: what do you already know about the word altogether?

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Math Fluency. Math Fluency means quick practice. I say a small sum, and you work it out and tell me the answer. It helps your brain get fast and sure with adding and taking away up to 10. You will need your fingers, or some small things like stones, buttons or dried beans. That is all. Here is what I expect from you: try each one yourself first, then tell me your answer AND how you got it. Saying how you worked it out is the important part! There are 12 questions, in three rounds of four. We go one at a time. Here comes question one. There are 3 dates in one bowl and 2 dates in another bowl. How many dates altogether?

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Unit Challenge. In this challenge you pick one big idea from Unit 5 — like adding, taking away, or number bonds — and you show it with real things you can touch. It is the last activity of the unit, so it is your chance to show what you know. Why do we do it? Because when you can show an idea and explain it out loud, it means you really understand it. Not just remembering — understanding! You will need paper, a pencil, and some small objects you can count. Stones, buttons, bottle caps, or dried beans all work well. A grown-up nearby can help you find them. There are four steps. I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Choose one idea from Unit 5. You can pick adding two groups together, adding 1 more, taking away, or number bonds. What I expect: just tell me which one you choose, and one sentence about what it means in your own words. Take your time — there's no rush. Which idea do you choose?

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Unit Overview for Unit 6: Position. Position means where something is — on, under, above, below, behind, in front of, and between. We are doing this overview so you know what our whole unit is about before we start. By the end of today you will know what we will learn, and you will already try one position word yourself. You will need three small things you can hold: a cup, a spoon, and one small toy. There are 4 steps, and I will give you one at a time. Here comes step one. Go and find your cup, your spoon, and your small toy, and put them in front of you. Tell me when you have them! 🙂

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text:
Hello! I'm your teacher today, and this is our Position lesson. Position means where something is. In this lesson you will learn the words that tell where things are: on, under, above, below, behind, in front of, next to and between. You will also learn order words like 1st, 2nd and 3rd. Why? Because these words help you tell people exactly where things are, like "my shoe is under the bed."

What I expect from you: get one small thing you can hold, like a toy, a stone or a spoon. Also get a cup or a box. Then tell me what you chose. You will move them and say the words out loud with me. There are 5 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Go and find your two things — one small object, and one cup or box. Tell me what you found. 😊

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Welcome to our Maths Words page! These are the special words we use to say where something is. Today we will learn them together, a few at a time. By the end, you will be able to use these words to tell someone exactly where a thing is — like "my shoe is under the bed". Here is what I expect from you: say each word out loud, and then make your OWN little sentence with it, about something real near you. That is how the word becomes yours. You will need one small thing you can hold — a toy, a spoon, a cup. Anything! There are 4 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: our first two words are on and under. On means it is sitting on top and touching. Under means it is tucked underneath. Put your small object ON a table or chair. Then move it UNDER. Tell me when you have done it. 🙂

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! I'm your teacher today. 😊

This activity is called Visual Models. We use real things you can touch to SHOW where something is. We do it because position words like on, under and between are much easier to feel than to just hear. By the end, you will be able to place an object and say where it is, all by yourself. What you need: a cup, a small toy or a stone, and a table or mat. Ask your grown-up to help you find them. What I expect from you: put the object where I say, then tell me the position word in a full sentence, like "The cup is on the mat."

There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Put your cup ON the table. Then tell me where it is, in a full sentence.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today we are learning about position. Position means where something is — like on, under, above, below, and between. We do this so you can say exactly where things are, and follow instructions like "put the cup under the mat". You will need one small thing you can hold — a cup, a toy, or a spoon. And something to put it on, like a chair or a table. There are six little steps. I will give you one at a time. What I want from you each time is to move your object, then tell me the position word in a full sentence. Here comes step one. Put your cup on the mat or the table. Now move it under the table. Where is the cup now? Tell me like this: "The cup is ___ the table."

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Hello! Let's start our Worked Examples. A worked example is a question that is already solved for us. We read it, and we watch how the thinking works. That way, you learn the smart way to think before you try on your own. Today we will do 4 examples together. By the end, you will be able to say where something is, using words like on, under, above and between. You need your ears, your voice, and maybe one small toy to move around. 🙂

Here comes step one. Duniya puts a bottle cap ON a stool. Then she moves it UNDER the stool. Before I show you the thinking, you have a go. Where is the bottle cap now? Just tell me the one word.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Guided Practice. In this activity you answer position questions — questions about where things are, like on, under, above, below, between and next to. We do it so those words become easy for you to say and use every day. Here is what I expect from you: say your answer out loud or type it, then tell me how you know. One word is fine, but I love hearing your thinking too. There are 12 questions, and we will do them one at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. Here comes question one. Duniya puts a bottle cap on a stool. Then she moves it under the stool. Where is the bottle cap now?

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Learn the Method. 📚

This is where we learn the words that tell us WHERE something is — like on, under, above, below and between. We do it with real things you can hold and move, because your hands help your brain remember. By the end, you will be able to put an object somewhere and say the right position word out loud. What you need: a small thing like a stone, a spoon or a toy, and something bigger like a cup, a plate or a stool. A grown-up can help you. We have 6 small steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Put your small thing ON top of your big thing. Then say it out loud in a full sentence, like this: "The stone is ON the plate."

I expect one sentence back from you, with the word ON in it. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me what you said!

games.label: Games
games.text:
Hello! Today we are playing the Position games. 🎲

These games ask you short questions about where things are — words like on, under, above and below. We play them so those words become quick and easy in your head. You need to get 3 right to win a game. Here is what I expect from you: read each question, tell me your answer, and then tell me why you picked it. Guessing is okay, but thinking out loud is even better! There are 4 rounds in our first game. Here comes question one. A cup is resting on top of a table, touching the table. Where is the cup — on the table, or under the table?

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today we are doing Math Fluency. That means quick practice with our position words — the words that tell us where something is, like on, under, above and below. We do this so the words come to you fast, without stopping to think hard. Here is what I expect from you: answer with the position word, and then tell me how you knew. Take your time — there's no rush. There are 4 questions in Round 1. Here comes question one. Duniya puts a bottle cap ON a stool. Then she moves it UNDER the stool. Where is the bottle cap now?

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today we are doing the "Practise together" activity for Unit 6, Position. In this activity you will pick one position idea, make it real with a drawing or with toys, and teach it to someone in your family. We do this because you learn a word best when you can show it and say it. By the end, you will be able to show a position word and make your own question about it. You will need paper, a pencil, and a few small things you can hold, like a toy, a cup, or a spoon. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Choose ONE position idea from our unit. You could pick on, under, above, below, behind, in front of, next to, or between. You could also pick ordinal numbers, like 1st, 2nd, 3rd. Pick just one, and tell me which one you chose. 😊

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Unit Challenge. 🌟

This challenge is where you show off your position words — words like on, under, above, below, between, and first, second, third. You will make something you can see and touch, then teach it to someone in your family. Teaching someone else is the best way to know you really understand it! Get ready with paper, a pencil, and a few small things from your home — a cup, a spoon, a toy, a stone. There are 4 steps, and I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Pick ONE position word from this unit that you like best. It could be under, or between, or above. Just choose one and tell me which one you picked.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! I'm your teacher today. 😊

This page is called Explain Your Thinking. Here you don't just say the answer — you say WHY. Talking about your thinking helps the words like on, under, above and below stick in your brain. You will need your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want help typing. What I expect from you: try to use a whole sentence, and use one position word in it. Short is fine! Mistakes are how we learn. There are 3 small steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Picture this in your head. A boat is floating on the water. A fish is swimming down in the water, under the boat. It is not touching the boat. Tell me one word that says where the fish is compared to the boat.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Welcome to Solve Real Problems! 🌟

This page gives us little stories from real life — home, the market, a bus trip. In each one, you use our position words like under, next to, between, and our order words like 1st, 2nd, 3rd. We do this because position words are not just for books. You use them every day when you tidy your shoes or stand in a line. Here is what I expect from you: say your answer, then tell me one small reason why. Even a few words is perfect. There are 6 problems. We will do one at a time. Here comes question one. At home, Amina washes her hands, then eats anjero, then brushes her teeth. Which one does she do 1st?

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today we are learning our maths words for this unit. These are the special words we use when we put things into groups. Knowing them helps you understand every question in Unit 7. By the end, you will be able to say each word and what it means, and use it in your own sentence. You will need a small pile of things you can move around — buttons, spoons, bottle caps, or even socks. A grown-up can help you find them. We will do three words together, in three steps. Step 1. Our first word is sort. Sort means to put things into groups using a rule. Now you try: put your pile of things into two groups. You choose the rule — maybe colour, maybe big and small. Tell me when you have done it, and tell me your two groups. 😊

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today we start Unit 7. It is called Statistics — that is a big word for sorting things into groups and counting them. We do this because sorting helps us see what is the same and what is different. By the end you will be able to make groups, count them, and say which group has more. This page is our Unit Overview. It is like looking at a map before a walk. There are 3 small steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Find a small pile of things you can move with your hands. Buttons, bottle caps, stones, or dry beans all work well. Try to get about 6 to 10 of them, in different colours or sizes. A good pile is one where the things are NOT all the same. You can ask your grown-up to help you find them. Tell me when you have your pile, and what you found! 🙂

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Today's lesson is called Statistics. That is a big word for a simple idea: putting things into groups so we can understand them. We are doing this because sorting helps us answer questions like "how many?" and "which has more?" By the end, you will be able to sort things into groups, count them, and use a sorting circle. You will need a small pile of little things you can move with your hands — buttons, stones, bottle caps, or dry beans. Ask your grown-up to help you find some. Different colours or sizes is best! There are 4 steps. Here is step 1. Go and get about 8 small things and put them in a pile in front of you. Tell me what you found. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today we are exploring sorting. Sorting means putting things into groups. A group of things that belong together is called a set. By the end you will be able to sort things, count them, and say which group has more. You will need your eyes, your thinking, and if you can, a small pile of buttons or beans or bottle caps beside you. A grown-up can help you find them. There are six little steps. Here comes step one. Look at a pile of buttons. Some are red. Some are not red. We put the red ones in one pile and the rest in another pile. My question for you: what do all the buttons in the red pile have in common? I am hoping for a short sentence, in your own words. Take your time — there's no rush.

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today we are learning the method for sorting. Sorting means putting things into groups. A group is called a set. By the end, you will be able to sort a pile of things into two sets, and say your rule out loud. You will need a small pile of things you can touch. Buttons, bottle caps, stones, beans, or even socks. Ask your grown-up to help you find some. Our first method has three steps. Here comes step one. Step one: tip your small pile of things onto the table or the mat in front of you. Spread them out a little so you can see each one. I expect you to have about six to ten things, all mixed up, not in a neat line. Tell me when your pile is ready, and tell me what things you chose. 😊

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today we are looking at the picture models for sorting. A model is just a way to SEE the maths with real things you can touch. We do this so sorting stops being words and becomes something your hands can do. By the end, you will be able to make two sets, count them, and say which set has more. You will need a small pile of little things: buttons, bottle caps, beans, or even socks! A grown-up can help you find them. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Go and get about 8 small things in a pile on a table or mat. Mix them up. Some should look different from the others, like different colours or different sizes. Tell me when you have your pile, and tell me what things you chose.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Hello! Today we are on the Worked Examples page. A worked example is a maths problem that shows you every step, like watching someone tie a shoe before you try it. We do this so you can see how good sorting works, step by step. By the end, you will be able to sort a pile of things into two groups and say your rule out loud. You will need one thing: a small pile of objects. Buttons, bottle caps, stones, or even socks. Ask your grown-up to help you find some. 😊

There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Get your pile ready. Put about 6 objects in front of you, and make sure they are not all the same colour. Tell me what you found and what colours they are.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text:
Hello! Today we are doing Guided Practice for our Statistics unit. In this activity, you will sort things into groups, count them, and say which group has more. Sorting means putting things that are the same together. A group like that is called a set. We do this because sorting helps us understand what we see. It is the very first step of statistics. What I expect from you: try each question yourself first, then tell me your answer AND how you got it. Numbers first, rules later — let's count it out. 😊

We have three parts today: sorting, counting, and comparing. Here comes question one. Amina has 6 bottle caps. 4 are silver and 2 are gold. She sorts them into "silver" and "not silver". How many caps go in the silver set? How many go in the not-silver set?

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Hello! Today we are doing the "Practise together" activity. You will pick one idea from our sorting unit, make it real with objects or a drawing, and then teach it to someone at home. We do this because explaining an idea out loud is how it really sticks in your brain. You will need paper, a pencil, and a few small things from home — buttons, spoons, stones, or bottle caps. There are four steps. I will give you one at a time. 🙂

Step one: choose one idea from this unit to show. You could choose sorting things into two sets, or counting and comparing two sets, or a sorting circle (a Venn diagram). A good choice is one you can show with real objects on a table. Which idea do you want to pick?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Welcome to Solve Real Problems! 🌟

In this activity, we take sorting out of the classroom and into real life — the kitchen, the market, a walk outside. You will sort real things into two groups, count them, and say which group has more. We do this because sorting helps us every day. Tidying toys, matching socks, counting plates — that is maths! What I expect from you: try each one before I help, and always tell me your thinking, not just your answer. There are 6 problems. Here comes question one. At home, Amina has 9 clothes pegs. 5 are wooden and 4 are plastic. She sorts them by what they are made of. How many pegs are in each set?

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the Unit 7 games. These are little sorting challenges — you read a question, then pick the best answer from four choices. We do this because playing helps the ideas stick. By the end you will be quicker at sorting things into sets, and at saying which set has more. Here is what I expect from you: read each question twice, then tell me your answer AND why you picked it. The "why" is the important part! There are 4 steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Look at your Games page. Find the first game, called "Quick Match: Sort." Click it to open it. Tell me when it is open. 🙂

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Math Fluency. 😊

Here is what it is. I will give you short sorting questions, one at a time. You answer, and I will tell you how you did. Why do we do it? Because sorting gets quick and easy when we practise it, just like tying your shoes. What I expect from you: try each one on your own first, tell me your answer, and tell me how you worked it out. Guessing is fine — thinking out loud is even better! You will need a pencil and paper, or just some small things near you, like buttons, beans or bottle caps. There are 4 questions in Round 1. Here comes question one. You have 5 buttons. 3 of them are red. 2 of them are blue. The rule is: red / not red. How many buttons go in the red pile?

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Welcome to your Unit Challenge! This is where you show off everything you learned about sorting. You will pick one big idea from this unit, make a model of it, tell a family member about it, and then write your very own question. It helps you show that you really understand sorting, sets, and more and fewer. You will need paper, a pencil, and some small things from home — buttons, spoons, stones, or bottle caps. There are four steps. I will give you one at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Choose one idea from this unit. You can pick sorting into two sets, comparing which set has more, or the sorting circle (Venn diagram). Tell me which idea you choose, and say it in your own words. 😊

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Explain Your Thinking". In this activity you do not just give an answer — you say HOW you worked it out, in your own words. We do this because explaining is what turns moving buttons around into real maths. By the end you will be able to say your sorting rule out loud in a clear sentence. All you need is your thinking voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby to listen. There are 3 steps. Here is step 1. Read this question with me: "You sorted 8 buttons into two piles using the rule shiny / not shiny. Explain how you decided which pile each button belonged to."

Now tell me one thing only: what does the word "shiny" help you check about each button?

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Welcome to Unit 8! This page is our Unit Overview. It is like looking at a map before a trip — we see what we will learn about time before we start. By the end of this little activity, you will know the three big things this unit teaches, and you will have told me one thing you already know. All you need is your voice and your thinking brain. A pencil is nice if you want to draw. There are 4 short steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Look at the word "Time" at the top of your page. Tell me one place you have seen a clock. Maybe on a wall, a phone, or an oven? A good answer is just a few words, like "on our kitchen wall". Tell me when you have one.

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text:
Welcome to our lesson on Time! 🕐

This lesson teaches you two big things. First, the days of the week and the parts of a day. Second, how to read a clock. By the end, you will be able to say the seven days in order and read o'clock and half past times all by yourself. You need your voice, and a pencil and paper if you have one. A grown-up nearby can help too. There are 5 steps. Let's start with step 1. Step 1: The days of the week. A week is a group of 7 days. Here they are in order:
Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Now you try. Say them out loud, and type them here for me in the right order, starting with Monday. Take your time — there's no rush.

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Maths Words page. This page holds the special time words for Unit 8, like clock, o'clock and half past. We learn them first, because when you know the words, reading a clock becomes easy. By the end, you will be able to say each word and use it in your own sentence. You need your voice, and a pencil if you like writing. We will do three rounds, three words each round. Here comes step one, our first three words. Week means a group of 7 days. Today, tomorrow, yesterday means now, the next day, the day before. Before and after tell us which thing comes first and which comes next. Now you try. Tell me: how many days are in one week? 😊

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Hello! Today we are learning about time. ⏰

This page is called Explore the Concept. It gives you six little questions to think about. We will do them one at a time, together. By the end you will know the days of the week, the parts of the day, and how to read a clock. What you need: just your thinking brain, and maybe a pencil. What I expect from you: try your best answer, even if you are not sure. Mistakes are how we learn. Here comes question one. Say the days of the week out loud, starting with Monday. Then tell me: what day comes right after Monday?

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models activity. 🙂

A visual model is a picture that helps us see an idea. On this page we have five pictures about time: the days of the week, the parts of a day, the two hands on a clock, o'clock times, and half past times. We do this because time is easier to understand when we can see it, not just hear it. By the end, you will be able to look at a clock and say the time. You will need a pencil, some paper, and your voice for saying things out loud. I expect you to try each step yourself first, and tell me what you see. There are five steps, one for each picture. Step 1. Look at the days of the week model on your screen. Say all seven days out loud, in order, from Monday. Then type them to me. Take your time — there's no rush.

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Learn the Method."

This page shows us HOW to do time things, step by step. We are doing it so you can name the days of the week and read a clock all by yourself. By the end, you will be able to say the days in order and point to the two clock hands. You will need: a pencil, some paper, and your voice. Cut seven small pieces of paper if you can — a grown-up can help. There are 6 methods on this page. We will do them one at a time. Here comes the first one! Method 1: Ordering the Days of the Week. Step 1: Take seven little papers. On each one, write one day of the week. Lay them in a line, from Monday to Sunday. I expect to see seven cards in one line, in the right order. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when your line is ready! 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Welcome to Guided Practice! This is where we try Time questions together, one at a time. We do it so the days of the week and the clock start to feel easy, not tricky. Here is what I expect from you: give me your answer, then tell me how you got it. Guessing is fine — telling me your thinking is even better. Mistakes are how we learn. You will need a pencil, some paper, and your voice for saying days out loud. There are 12 questions, and we will go through them slowly. Here comes question one. Say the days of the week out loud, in order, starting with Monday. Count them on your fingers as you say them. Then type them here for me.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Hello! Let me be your teacher for this page. 😊

This page is called Worked Examples. That means we look at a time question, and I show you how a good thinker works it out, step by step. We do this so you learn the WAY to think, not just the answer. By the end, you will be able to say the days in order and read a clock. All you need is your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. We will do 4 examples together, one at a time. Here comes step one. Step 1. Put these days in order: Wednesday, Monday, Friday, Tuesday. What I expect from you: don't just guess. Say the whole week out loud first, from Monday, and use it to help you. Then tell me your four days in order. Take your time — there's no rush.

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Welcome! Today's activity is called Practise together. You will pick one idea from our Time unit and make it real — you will draw or build it with your own hands. Then you will teach it to someone in your family. We do this because teaching something is the best way to remember it forever. You need paper, a pencil, and maybe a few things from home, like a plate or bottle caps. A grown-up can help you find them. There are four steps. Here is step one. Step one: choose ONE idea from this unit. You could choose the days of the week, the parts of the day (morning, afternoon, evening), or the clock with its two hands. A good choice is the one you find most interesting. Which one do you choose?

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Welcome to Math Fluency! This is our quick practice game about time. I will ask you short, snappy questions about days and clocks. We do this so the answers come to you fast, without stopping to think hard. By the end, you will say the days of the week and read clock hands quickly and surely. You need nothing but your voice and your thinking brain. There are 12 questions in 3 rounds. I ask one, you answer, then we go on. Take your time — there's no rush. Here comes question one. Say the day that comes after Friday.

games.label: Games
games.text:
Welcome to our Games page! These games are little time challenges. Each game gives you four quick questions about time — days of the week, parts of the day, and clock hands.
