We play them because playing helps your brain remember. By the end, you will name the days in order and know which clock hand is which, fast, without stopping to think. You need only your voice, your fingers for counting, and your thinking brain. 🙂

Here is what I expect from you: try each answer yourself first, and tell me WHY you picked it. A guess is fine — but tell me your thinking too. We will play the first game together. It is called Quick Match: Week. It has 4 rounds. Here comes question one. How many days are there in a week? Is it 7, 6, 5, or 8?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Welcome to Solve Real Problems! 🌟

In this activity we use what we know about time in real life. Days of the week, morning and evening, the clock — all the things you have been learning. We do this because time words are not just for school. You use them at home, at the market, everywhere. There are 6 problems. I will give you one at a time. I expect you to tell me your answer AND how you worked it out. Saying the days out loud on your fingers is a great way to think. Here comes question one. At home, Amina's mother writes the day on a small board each morning. Yesterday she wrote "Sunday". What day should she write today? Take your time — there's no rush.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Welcome to Explain Your Thinking! 🌟

In this activity you do not just say the answer. You say HOW you worked it out. This is the part where you talk like a real mathematician. Why do we do it? Because when you can explain your thinking, the idea sticks in your head for good. There are 6 questions. We will do one at a time. You need your talking voice, and a pencil if you like writing. What I expect from you: a good answer has two parts. Part one, the answer. Part two, the words "I know because..." Say your thinking out loud, even if it feels slow. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose. Here comes question one. Today is Sunday. What day will tomorrow be, and how do you know?

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Unit Challenge. 🌟

This is the last activity in our Time unit. It has 12 questions about days of the week, parts of the day, and reading clocks. We do it to show what you have learned — it is like a little show-and-tell for your brain! By the end, you will know which time skills are strong and which need one more practice. Here is what I expect from you. Read each question twice. Think before you tap. And because this one is graded, I will not give you answers — but I will help you get ready and cheer you on. There are 4 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Get ready. Sit somewhere quiet, and have a pencil and paper near you. If you have a toy clock or a paper clock, put that next to you too. Tell me when you are ready.

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Unit Overview for Unit 9: Numbers to 20. An overview means a first look. We peek at what we will learn, before we learn it. By the end of this activity you will know the big ideas of this unit, and you will already have counted past ten. You need your voice, and a pencil and paper if you have one. A grown-up can sit with you too. There are four steps. Here comes step one. Step one: count out loud from one all the way to twenty. Go slowly. If you get stuck after ten, that is fine — just tell me where you stopped. I expect you to say every number, with no skipping. Type the numbers here when you are done.

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Welcome to our lesson, Unit 9: Numbers to 20! In this lesson we learn to count all the way to 20. We do it because numbers past ten help us count real things — goats, dates, buttons, friends. By the end, you will count to 20, say the teen names, and know that a teen number is one ten and some ones. You need a pencil, some small things you can hold (stones, beans or buttons), and your counting voice. We have 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Count out loud from 1 all the way to 20. Say every number slowly, and touch a finger or a stone for each one. What I expect: no numbers skipped, and a clear "eleven, twelve, thirteen" — those are the tricky ones. Type the numbers here so I can see them. Take your time — there's no rush.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today we are on the Explore page for Unit 9, Numbers to 20. In this activity we look at big ideas about numbers past ten, one at a time, and you answer a little question for each one. We do it so counting to twenty becomes as easy as counting to ten. By the end, you will count to 20 forwards and backwards, and know that a teen number is one ten and some ones. You will need a pencil, some paper, and maybe 20 small things like beans, buttons or stones. There are 6 short steps. Step 1. Let's count on to 20. You already count to 10, so we just keep going. Say this out loud with a grown-up if one is nearby: ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty. Then tell me: what number comes right after 12?

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for our Math Words page. This page is our word box for Unit 9. It holds the special maths words we use when we count to 20. We learn them so that when I say "one ten and six ones", you know exactly what I mean. By the end you will be able to say each word and use it yourself. You need your voice, and a pencil and paper if you like. Your grown-up can sit with you too. We have four steps. Here comes step one. Step one: the word teen numbers. Teen numbers are the numbers 11 to 19. Say them with me: eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen. Now you try: is 15 a teen number? Tell me yes or no. 😊

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Learn the Method. A method is a step-by-step way of doing something. On this page we learn six little methods for numbers up to 20. By the end, you will be able to count to 20 forwards and backwards, say the teen number names, write them, and show a number as one ten and some ones. You will need a pencil, some paper, and about ten to twenty small things you can move — beans, stones, buttons or bottle caps. A grown-up can help you find them. I expect you to try each step out loud or with your hands, then tell me what happened. Talking to me is part of the work! Here comes step one. Method 1 is Counting Forward and Backward to 20. On your paper, write the numbers 0 to 20 in one long line, with a little space between each one. That is your number track. Tell me when it is ready. 😊

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Worked Examples. A worked example is a maths question with the whole answer shown, step by step. We look at them together so you can see HOW a good mathematician thinks, not just the answer. By the end you will be able to count to 20, say the teen number names, and show a teen number as one ten and some ones. You need a pencil, some paper, and 20 small things you can count — beans, buttons, stones or bottle tops. A grown-up can help you gather them. We have 4 steps today. Here comes step one. Step 1: Counting to 20. Write these numbers on your paper, and fill in the three gaps:
12, 13, ___, 15, ___, 17, 18, ___, 20

What I expect: you say each number out loud as you count on from 12, and you write three numbers in the gaps. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me your three numbers when you are done.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our lesson. Visual Models means pictures that show a number. A ten-frame is a box with ten spaces. When it is full, that is one ten. We use these pictures because seeing a number helps you understand it, not just say it. What I expect from you: try each step out loud, and tell me your answer even if you are not sure. Mistakes are how we learn. You will need a pencil, paper, and about 20 small things — beans, buttons, stones, or bits of pasta. A grown-up can help you find them. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Draw two boxes on your paper. Each box should have 10 spaces inside, like an egg carton — 5 spaces on top, 5 spaces underneath. These are your two ten-frames. Tell me when your two frames are drawn. 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text:
Hello! Today we are doing Guided Practice for Numbers to 20. That means we will do some questions together, one at a time. I ask, you think, then you tell me your answer. By the end you will be able to count to 20, say the teen numbers, and know that a teen number is one ten and some ones. You need your pencil, some paper, and your good thinking voice. Take your time — there's no rush. There are four steps today. Here comes step one. Count out loud from 11 to 20. Then tell me the missing numbers here:

11, ___, 13, ___, 15, 16, ___, 18, ___, 20

I am looking for four numbers, in order. Say them slowly. 😊

games.label: Games
games.text: Welcome to the Games page! These are quick number games about our Unit 9 numbers to 20. We play them to make counting fast and easy, so teen numbers feel as simple as counting to ten. Each game has 4 short rounds. You need to get 3 right to win the game. Here is what I expect from you: say your answer out loud or type it, and then tell me how you worked it out. Guessing is not the game — thinking is. You can use your fingers or draw a number line if that helps. There are 4 rounds. Let's start with the game called Quick Match: Teen numbers. Here comes question one. What number comes right after 16? Your choices are: 15, 17, 18, 20.

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today we are doing the "Practise together" activity for Unit 9, Numbers to 20. In this activity you pick one big idea from our unit, then make it real — you build it or draw it. Then you teach it to someone in your family. Teaching someone else is the best way to show you really know it! By the end, you will be able to show a number to 20 and explain it in your own words. Get ready: paper, a pencil, and some small things you can count — buttons, stones, beans, or bottle caps. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Choose one idea from this unit. You could choose counting to 20, or teen numbers as one ten and some ones, or comparing two numbers. A good choice is one you find interesting — not just the easy one! Which idea do you choose? Tell me. 😊

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text:
Welcome to Math Fluency! This is our quick-thinking practice for Unit 9, Numbers to 20. Fluency means saying the answer quickly and surely, without stopping to worry. We do it so the numbers 11 to 20 feel as easy as 1 to 10. By the end, you will count forwards, count backwards, and say the teen numbers with a big smile. You need your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. There are 3 rounds, with a few quick questions in each. I will give you one at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. Round 1, question one. Count forward: 10, 11, 12, ___, ___

What are the next two numbers?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today we are doing Solve Real Problems. These are little number stories about real life — goats, mangoes, buses and buttons. We do this so your counting to 20 works outside the book, in the real world. By the end, you will count forwards and backwards to 20 inside a story. You need your ears, your fingers for counting, and maybe a pencil. There are 6 problems. Here comes question one. At home, Amina lines up 20 buttons. She takes one away at a time. She counts backward: 20, 19, 18, and then... what number comes next? I would like you to say the number, and tell me how you knew. Take your time — there's no rush.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Explain Your Thinking."

In this activity you do not just give an answer. You tell me HOW you worked it out, in your own words. We do this because a mathematician can explain their thinking, not only say a number. By the end, you will be able to talk about teen numbers like a real maths teacher! You need your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Count out loud, starting at 9, all the way to 20. Say every number, slowly. A good answer misses no numbers — especially around fifteen and sixteen. Type your counting here when you are ready. Take your time — there's no rush.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Welcome to your Unit Challenge! 🌟

This is your big finish for Unit 9: Numbers to 20. You will pick one idea from this unit, make a model of it, explain it out loud, and then write your very own maths question. We do this because when you can show an idea and teach it to someone, it really sticks in your brain. You will need paper, a pencil, some small things to count (stones, buttons, beans or dates), and a grown-up or family member nearby to listen. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Choose ONE idea from this unit. You could choose teen numbers as one ten and some ones, or counting to 20, or comparing two numbers, or odd and even. Tell me which idea you pick, and why you picked it.

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Unit 10: 3D Shapes. 🎲

This first page is our Unit Overview. It is like looking at a map before a trip. We will see what we will learn, and get our things ready. By the end of this unit, you will be able to name solid shapes like the cube, sphere and cylinder, and say which ones roll and which ones stack. There are 4 small steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Go and find a cube. A cube is a solid shape with 6 flat square sides, all the same. A die from a game, a stock cube, or a small square block will all work. You can ask your grown-up to help you find one. When you have it in your hand, tell me what you found.

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text:
Hello! Today we are learning our shape words for this unit. 📦

This page has the special words we use for solid shapes, like face, edge and cube. Learning these words means you can say exactly what you see, not just "that round thing". Here is what I expect from you: try each word out loud, and tell me one real thing from your home that matches. You will need your voice and maybe a grown-up nearby. We will do this in 4 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Say this word out loud — 3D shape. It means a solid shape that takes up space, and you can hold it in your hands. Now go and find ONE solid thing near you and hold it. What did you pick?

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Unit 10: 3D Shapes. 3D shapes are solid shapes. You can pick them up and hold them. A ball, a tin and a box are all 3D shapes. By the end of this lesson you will be able to name them, count their flat faces, and say which ones roll and which ones stack. Here is what I expect from you: pick things up and really look at them, count out loud, and tell me your answer each time. Guessing is fine — mistakes are how we learn. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Go and find three things. A ball (or an orange), a tin (or a cup), and a box (or a die, or a stock cube). You can ask your grown-up to help you find them. Tell me when you have them, and tell me what you found. 😊

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Welcome to our shape lesson! 😊

This activity is called Explore the Concept. We will look at solid shapes — shapes you can hold in your hand, like a ball or a box. We do it so you can name them and say why some roll and some stack. By the end, you will be able to point around your room and name the shapes you see. You will need a few things from home: a ball or an orange, a box, a tin, and a piece of paper. You can ask your grown-up to help you get them. There are 5 small steps. Here comes step one! Step 1: Hold the ball or orange in one hand. Hold the flat piece of paper in the other hand. I want you to tell me: which one is the 3D shape? A 3D shape is solid and takes up space. Tell me which one, and how you can tell. Take your time — there's no rush.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today we are on the Visual Models page. These are pictures that help you SEE what a 3D shape is. We do this because holding and looking beats just remembering words. By the end, you will be able to name solid shapes like cube, sphere and cylinder, and say why they roll or stack. You need your eyes, your hands, and one real object from home if you can find one. A grown-up can help you fetch it. There are six little models. We will do one at a time. Here comes step one. Look at Model 1: solid shapes take up space. Find one thing you can hold in your hand, like a ball, a tin or a box. Then tell me what you found, and tell me if it feels flat or solid. Take your time — there's no rush.

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Learn the Method". A method is just a set of small steps we follow. On this page we learn how to look at solid shapes and name them. By the end, you will be able to pick up a real thing at home and say its shape name out loud. You will need a few things from around your home: a ball, a tin, a box, and a die or a small block. Ask your grown-up to help you find them. 🙂

Here is what I expect from you: touch each object, look at it carefully, and tell me what you see in your own words. Guessing is fine — mistakes are how we learn. There are 6 short steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Go and collect your objects. Put them all on the table in front of you. Tell me when they are ready, and tell me what you found.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Hello! Today we are on the Worked Examples page. A worked example shows how a maths thinker solves a shape puzzle, step by step. We do this so you learn the thinking, not just the answer. By the end, you will be able to name solid shapes like cube, sphere and cylinder — and say HOW you knew. Here is what I expect from you: try each one first in your own words, then tell me your reason. Saying "because..." is the most important part! 😊

You will need one real thing from home if you can: a die, a small box, a ball, or a tin. Ask your grown-up to help you find one. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Amina finds a ball on the table. Tell me what shape a ball is, and finish this sentence: "It is a ball shape because it is ______."

Take your time — there's no rush.

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today we are doing our "Practise together" activity about 3D shapes. 3D shapes are solid shapes you can hold, like a ball or a box. In this activity you will make or draw one shape, then teach it to someone in your family. By the end, you will be able to name a 3D shape and say why it looks that way. You need paper, a pencil, and a few things from your home — like a tin, a box, or a ball. There are 4 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Pick ONE shape from this unit to be your special shape today. You can choose cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone or pyramid. I expect you to tell me your shape name, and one real thing in your home that has that shape. Which shape do you choose? 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Guided Practice. 😊

This is where we practise the solid shapes we have been learning — cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone. Practice helps the shape names stick in your head. By the end, you will be able to look at a real thing and say its shape name. Here is what I expect from you: try each one out loud or type your answer, and tell me WHY you think so. A guess is fine — but always tell me your reason. You will need one thing: a small cube, like a die or a square block. A ball and a tin would be nice too. Ask your grown-up to help you find them. We have 5 steps. Here comes step one. Look at a ball, or a football. Is it a 3D shape or a 2D shape? Tell me how you know.

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Math Fluency. 😊

This activity is quick shape practice. I say an object, you say its 3D shape name — fast, like a game. We do it so the shape names come to you straight away, without stopping to think. Here is what I expect from you: answer in your own words, and if you can, tell me one small reason why. A wrong answer is fine — mistakes are how we learn. There are 12 quick questions, in 3 rounds of 4. If you have a ball, a tin, a die or a box near you, keep them close. Ready? Here comes question one. Hold a football in your hand. What 3D shape is it?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today we are doing "Solve Real Problems" — shape puzzles about real things, like a football, a tin, and a lunch box. We do this so you can spot 3D shapes all around your home, not just on paper. There are 6 little problems. I will give you one at a time. You tell me your answer AND how you know — that "how you know" part is what I really want to hear. Here comes question one. Amina picks up a football from under the bed. What 3D shape is the football, and how does she know?

games.label: Games
games.text: Welcome to our Games page! These are quick shape games. Each game asks you four little questions about 3D shapes — the solid shapes you can hold, like a ball or a box. We play these to make the shape names stick in your head, so you can say them fast without stopping to think. By the end you will name shapes like cube, sphere and cylinder all by yourself. Here is what I expect from you: tell me your answer AND tell me why you picked it. "Why" is the important part! If you can, grab a die or a small box and a ball to hold. We will do the first game together. It has 4 questions. Here comes question one. Which of these is the same shape as a football? Cube, sphere, cone, or cuboid?

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Welcome to your Unit Challenge! 🎉

This is the big finish for our 3D shapes unit. You will pick one idea from the unit, make a little model of it, and teach it to someone at home. This shows me that you really know your solid shapes — not just the names, but what they do. You will need paper, a pencil, and a few things from around your home. Good things to grab: a ball, a tin, a box, a die, a party hat. There are 4 steps. We do one at a time, and I will wait for you after each one. Step 1: Choose your idea. Pick ONE thing from this unit that you liked best. It could be naming 3D shapes, counting faces on a cube, or sorting shapes into rolls and stacks. Tell me which one you choose, and why you picked it. 😊

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Explain Your Thinking."

In this activity you do not just give a short answer. You say WHY, in your own words. This helps you really understand 3D shapes, not just remember names. All you need is your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. Here is what I expect from you: a full sentence, using shape words like solid, flat, face, curved surface. Do not worry about spelling. Thinking out loud is the win. There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Get a tin from your kitchen if you can, or just picture one. A real tin, and a picture of a tin printed on the label, look alike. Tell me: why is the real tin a 3D shape, but the picture is a 2D shape? Take your time — there's no rush.

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Welcome! This is our Unit Overview. It is like looking at a map before a trip. In this unit we learn about halves. A half is one of two equal parts of a whole. By the end, you will be able to fold a shape into two halves, share things fairly between two, and say what half of 6 or 8 is. You will need one piece of paper and a pencil. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 4 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Say this sentence out loud, and tell me what you think it means: "A half is one of two equal parts."

What do you think the word equal means?

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text:
Hello! Today's lesson is all about halves. 🙂

A half means one of two equal parts of a whole. We are learning this so we can share things fairly, like a biscuit or some dates. By the end, you will be able to tell if two parts are really halves, cut a shape into halves, and find half of a small number. You will need a piece of paper, a pencil, and about 10 small things like stones, beans or buttons. A grown-up can help you get them. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Take your piece of paper. Fold it so one side lies exactly on top of the other side. Then open it up and look. I expect you to tell me one thing: do the two sides match exactly, or does one side stick out?

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text:
Welcome! Today we are learning the special maths words for halves. 📘

This page is our word list. Learning these words helps you understand every question in this unit, because the questions use these exact words. By the end, you will be able to say what each word means in your own way, and use it in a sentence. You need your voice, and one small snack or a piece of paper you can fold. There are 4 steps. Step 1: Our first word is WHOLE. A whole means the complete thing, before it is cut or shared. A whole banana. A whole biscuit. A whole piece of paper. Now your turn. Look around you and tell me one whole thing you can see. Say it in a sentence, like this: "I can see a whole ____."

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Hello! Today we are exploring halves. 🙂

This activity gives you little thinking questions about halves. You look, you think, and you tell me your answer. By the end, you will know exactly what makes something a half — and it is one special word. You need your eyes, your brain, and maybe a piece of paper and a pencil. There are six little questions. I will give you one at a time, and I will wait for you. Here comes question one. You break a biscuit into two pieces. One piece is big. One piece is tiny. Are those two pieces halves? Tell me yes or no — and tell me why you think so.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! I'm your teacher today. 😊

This page is called Visual Models. That means little pictures that show us what a half looks like. We look at pictures because a half is much easier to see than to say. By the end you will be able to look at any picture and say "yes, that is a half" or "no, that is not a half". You need one piece of paper and a pencil next to you. There are five pictures, so five little steps. Ready? Here comes step one. Step 1: Look at the first model on your page. It shows one whole thing split into two parts. Tell me: are the two parts the same size, or is one bigger?

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Welcome to Learn the Method! 📄

This page shows us HOW to make halves — real ways we can do it with our hands. We do this so you can prove two parts are equal, not just guess with your eyes. By the end, you will be able to fold, check, and draw a line to make two halves. You will need one piece of paper and a pencil. A grown-up can help you tear or cut. What I expect from you: try each step for real with your paper, then tell me what you see. Short answers are fine! There are 6 methods on this page. We will do them one at a time. Method 1 is called Fold to Make Two Equal Halves. Step one: take one whole piece of paper and hold it flat. Tell me when you are holding it. 🙂

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Welcome! Today we are on the Worked Examples page for halves. A worked example is a maths story with the thinking shown. We read the story, think about it ourselves first, then check the good way to solve it. This helps you learn HOW to think, not just the answer. By the end, you will be able to say what a half really is, and prove two parts are equal. You need: a pencil, some paper, and if you can, a piece of paper you can fold. You can ask your grown-up to help you get these. 🙂

We will do four examples together, one at a time. Here comes step one. Amina has one anjero (one flat round bread). She tears it into two pieces. One piece is big. One piece is small. Are these two pieces halves? Tell me yes or no, and tell me why you think so.

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today we are doing the "Practise together" activity. It is about halves — a half is one of two equal parts of a whole. You will make something you can see and touch, then teach it to someone in your family. Teaching someone else is the best way to make an idea stick. You need paper, a pencil, and a few small things like stones, beans or toys. There are 4 steps. I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Choose one idea from our unit to show. You could choose halving a shape, like folding a paper circle. Or you could choose half of a set, like sharing 6 dates between 2 plates. Which one do you want to do? Tell me your choice. 🙂

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! I'm your teacher today, and this is Guided Practice. Guided Practice is where you try questions about halves, and I help you as you go. We do it so the big idea sticks: a half is one of two EQUAL parts. Here is what I expect from you. Answer in your own words. Tell me WHY you think so — that part matters most. And it is fine to be wrong; that is how we learn. You will need a pencil, some paper, and maybe a few small things to count, like stones or beans. We start with the warm-up questions. Here comes question one. A circle is cut into two matching pieces. Is each piece a whole, or a half?

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the Unit 11 games about halves. A game is like a quick quiz, but fun. Each game has 4 little questions. Playing them helps you remember one big idea: a half is one of two equal parts. Here is what I expect from you. Answer each question in your own words, and then tell me WHY you chose it. Guessing is okay, but thinking out loud is better! You need nothing except your brain. If you have paper and a pencil nearby, that can help you draw. We will do 4 steps — one question each. Let's start with something small. Here comes question one. Which one shows a half: a circle cut into two equal parts, or a circle cut into one big part and one small part?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello! Today we are doing "Solve Real Problems". 😊

These are little stories about halves from real life — sharing food, cutting bread, pouring water. We do this so you can use halves at home, not just on paper. By the end, you will be able to find a half in a real story and say why it is fair. You need your thinking brain, and maybe a pencil. There are 6 stories. I will give you one at a time. Here is what I expect from you: don't just say the answer — tell me WHY. Always check the two parts are equal. Story one. Amina has one chapati for breakfast. She wants to share it fairly with her little brother, so they each get a half. How should she cut it? Take your time — there's no rush.

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text:
Hello! This page is Math Fluency. It gives you quick questions about halves, so your brain gets fast at them. We do it to practise one big idea: a half is one of two equal parts. By the end, you will spot halves quickly and know half of 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. What I expect from you: answer in your own words, and tell me WHY. A guess is fine, but I always want your thinking too. Take your time — there's no rush. You just need your eyes, your voice, and maybe 10 small things like stones, buttons or beans near you. 🙂

There are 12 questions, in 3 rounds. We'll do them one at a time. Here comes question one. Two biscuits get broken. Biscuit A breaks into two same-size pieces. Biscuit B breaks into one big piece and one tiny piece. Which biscuit has been cut into halves?

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Let's look at this page together. 😊

This activity is called "Explain Your Thinking." You read a question, and you say the answer in your own words. We do it because knowing an answer is good, but saying WHY is even better. By the end, you will be able to explain what a half is, all by yourself. What I expect from you: talk to me in your own words. Short is fine. You don't need perfect words — you need your thinking. If you have a grown-up nearby, they can help you type. There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Tell me what you already know about this. In your own words, what is a half?

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Welcome to your Unit Challenge! 🌟

This is the last part of Unit 11. It is a quiz all about halves. It checks that you can spot two equal parts, halve a shape, and find half of a small number. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe 10 small things like stones or buttons to help you count. Here is what I expect from you: read each question twice, think before you tap, and tell me WHY you chose your answer. I will not give you answers — but I will help you think. That's a promise. There are 12 questions. We will go one at a time. Step 1: Get your counters ready. Find about 10 small things — stones, beans, buttons, or bits of paper. Put them next to you. Tell me when you have them. 😊

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for our Unit Overview. 📏

This page is like a map of Unit 12: Measures (2). Measures means comparing things — how heavy, how much a cup holds, how long, and how hot or cold. We look at the map first so you know where we are going. By the end you will be able to say what this unit is about in your own words. You need your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. There are 4 short steps. Here comes step one! Look around your room. Find one thing that is heavy and one thing that is light. A good answer names two real things, like "my shoe is heavy, my sock is light."

Tell me your two things.

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Unit 12: Measures. In this lesson we learn how to compare things. We will say which is heavier, which holds more, which is longer, and which is hot or cold. By the end, you will be able to look at two things and say which is which, using the right words. You need your ears, your voice, and two hands. A pencil too, if you like. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Mass. Mass means how heavy something is. Find two things near you. One heavy, like a book or a shoe. One light, like a sock or a leaf. Hold one in each hand. Feel which hand is pulled down more. I expect you to tell me two things: what you are holding, and which one is heavier. Take your time — there's no rush.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today we are exploring Measures. That means comparing things — which one is heavier, which holds more, which is longer, and which is hot or cold. We do this because measuring starts with careful comparing. By the end, you will be able to look at two things and say which is heavier or lighter, and tell me why. I expect you to guess out loud, try things with your hands if you can, and tell me your thinking — even if you are not sure. Wrong guesses help us learn! There are 6 little steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Imagine you hold a stone in one hand and a leaf in the other hand. Which one is heavier? Tell me which one, and how you know.

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for our Maths Words page. This activity is about the special words we use in Unit 12, Measures. These words help you say exactly what you notice — like which bag is heavier, or which jug holds more. By the end, you will know what each word means and be able to use it in your own sentence. Here is what I expect from you. Say each word out loud, tell me what it means in your own words, and then make one sentence about something in your home. Your own words are better than copying mine! We have 4 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: our first three words. Mass means how heavy something is. Heavier means it has more mass. Lighter means it has less mass. Balance scale is a tool that tips down on the heavier side. Now your turn. Look around you and find two things — maybe a shoe and a sock. Tell me: which one is heavier, and which one is lighter?

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models page. 😊

These are picture models. They help us SEE measuring ideas, not just hear about them. By the end you will be able to say which thing is heavier, which holds more, which is longer, and if something is hot or cold. There are six little models, and we will do one at a time. You need your eyes, your two hands, and a grown-up nearby if you want to fetch objects. Here is what I expect from you: try each one out loud or with real things, then tell me your answer in a full sentence. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1 of 6: Mass, heavier and lighter. Find two things near you. One heavy, like a shoe or a book. One light, like a sock or a leaf. Hold one in each hand and close your eyes. Which hand is pulled down more? Tell me: "The ___ is heavier than the ___."

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Learn the Method."

A method is just a set of steps we follow, in order, every time. This one shows us how to compare two things and say which is heavier. We do it so you never have to guess — you can find out for real. By the end, you will be able to compare two objects and say the answer in a proper sentence. You need two things from around you: one heavy-ish thing (a stone, a shoe, a full cup) and one light thing (a leaf, a sock, a tissue). You can ask your grown-up to help you find them. There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Hold one object in each hand. Close your eyes and feel. Which hand is pulled down more? What I expect: tell me the two things you picked, and which one pulled your hand down more. Take your time — there's no rush.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Worked Examples. Worked examples are little problems with the thinking shown, so we can see HOW a good answer is made. We do them so that when you meet a new question, you already know the steps. By the end you will be able to say which thing is heavier, which holds more, and which is longer — and say why. You just need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. A pencil and paper if you like. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Picture a small stone in one hand and a dry leaf in the other hand. Close your eyes and imagine holding them. Tell me which one is heavier — and try to say it in a full sentence, like this: "The ... is heavier than the ..."

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Welcome to Guided Practice! Today we compare things. We will say which thing is heavier, which holds more, and which is longer. We do this so you can measure with your own hands and eyes, not just guess. By the end, you will be able to say "this one is heavier" and tell me why. You need your voice and your thinking brain. A pencil is nice too, but not needed. There are 12 little questions. I will give you one at a time. Answer in your own words, and always tell me WHY you think so — that part matters most. Here comes question one. You hold an orange in one hand and a small feather in the other. Which one is heavier?

activities.label: Activities
activities.text: Hello! Today's activity is called Practise together. You will pick one big idea from this unit — like heavier and lighter, or which container holds more — and make a little model of it with real things or a drawing. Then you will teach it to someone in your family. We do this because explaining something out loud is the best way to make it stick in your head. You will need paper, a pencil, and a few things from around your home, like a spoon, a cup, a stone or a sock. A grown-up can sit with you. There are 4 steps. I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Choose one idea from this unit. You could choose mass (heavier and lighter), capacity (holds more or less), length (longer and shorter), or temperature (hot, warm, cold). Tell me which one you pick. 🙂

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text:
Welcome to Math Fluency! 😊

This is our quick-thinking practice. I say a measuring question, and you tell me your answer fast — heavier, lighter, holds more, holds less. We do it so the measuring words become easy for you, like knowing your own name. Here is what I expect: try each one yourself first, and tell me WHY you chose it. Guessing is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 3 rounds, 4 questions in each. Let's start with Round 1. Here comes question one. You hold a small rock in one hand and a cotton ball in the other hand. Which one is lighter?

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today we are doing "Explain Your Thinking."

In this activity you do not just say the answer. You say WHY. You use your own words, like you are teaching a friend. By the end, you will be able to explain how a balance scale shows which thing is heavier. You just need your voice or your typing fingers. 😊

There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Read this question and just picture it in your head. A car and a bicycle are put on a balance scale. Tell me one thing you notice about these two things. Which one has more stuff packed inside it?

games.label: Games
games.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Games page. 🎲

These games are short question games about measuring. You will answer questions about heavier and lighter, and about which container holds more. Playing them helps the words stick in your head, so you can use them at home too. Here is what I expect from you: read each question, think for a moment, then tell me your answer AND why you chose it. Guessing is okay, but thinking out loud is better. The first game is called Quick Match: Mass. It has 4 questions. I will give you one at a time. Here comes question one. Which is heavier: a big pillow or a small brick? Take your time — there's no rush.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Unit Challenge. Here is what it is. You pick one big idea from Unit 12 — like heavier and lighter, or holds more, or longer and shorter — and you make it real with your own hands. You will draw it or build it, show it to someone at home, and then make up your own question about it. Why do we do this? Because when you can show an idea and teach it to someone else, it really becomes yours. What I expect from you: pick things you can actually touch at home, use our unit words (heavier, lighter, holds more, holds less, longer, shorter), and try your own thinking even if it feels wobbly. Mistakes are how we learn. You will need paper, a pencil, and a few things from around your home. There are 4 steps. Step 1: Choose your idea. Tell me which one you want to do — mass (heavier and lighter), capacity (holds more or less), or length (longer and shorter). Which one do you pick? 😊

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Welcome! Let's begin. 😊

This activity is called Solve Real Problems. You take the measuring words you have learned — heavier, lighter, holds more, taller — and use them in real places like home, the market, and a journey. We do this because measuring is something we really do every day, not just on paper. By the end, you will have answered six real-life questions, and said why each answer is right. What I expect from you: give your answer, then tell me one reason. "Because..." is the important part! You just need your thinking. A pencil is nice if you want to write. There are six steps, one question each. Here comes question one. At home, your family fills the bathtub for a bath, and fills the sink for washing hands. Which one holds more water?

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Welcome to Unit 13! This page is our map for the whole unit. It shows what we will learn: adding and taking away numbers up to 20. We do this first so you know where we are going. By the end of this page, you will know our big goal and have your counting things ready. You need a pencil, and about 20 small things you can count — dates, beans, stones, or bottle caps. There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Go and collect your 20 small countable things. Put them in a little pile in front of you. You can ask your grown-up to help you find them. What I expect: one pile, with about 20 things in it. They can be anything small, as long as they all fit in your hand. Tell me when your pile is ready. 🙂

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for The Lesson in Unit 13: Working with Numbers to 20. In this lesson we learn to add and take away numbers up to 20 — the quick, clever way. By the end, you will be able to count on to add, count back to take away, and show your hops on a number line. What you need: a pencil, some paper, and about 20 small things you can count. Dry beans, buttons, bottle caps or small stones are perfect. Go and get them now. Here is what I expect from you: try each step out loud, tell me your answer, and tell me HOW you got it. Mistakes are how we learn — I am not worried about those at all. There are 4 steps. Let's start with step 1. Step 1: Count on to add. Put 12 beans in one pile. Put 5 beans in another pile. Now, do NOT count the 12 again. Hold 12 in your head. Touch the 5 beans one at a time and count on: 13, 14... keep going. What number do you land on? Tell me when you have it.

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Hello! Today we are learning our Unit 13 maths words — the special words we use when we add and take away numbers up to 20. We learn them so that when you read a question, you know exactly what it is asking you to do. By the end, you will be able to say each word and what it means, in your own words. You need your voice, and a pencil and paper if you like. There are 4 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: three adding words. Add (or plus) means put two amounts together. Count on means start at a number and count forward. Total (or altogether) means the answer when you add. Here they are in one picture: you have 12 dates, you add 5 more, you count on 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, and the total is 17. Now your turn. Tell me what "count on" means, in your own words. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Explore the Concept. 👋

This activity gives you six little thinking questions about adding and taking away up to 20. We do it so you learn the smart way to add: start at the bigger number and count on. By the end, you will know which way to hop on a number line, and how to split a number into two parts. You will need a pencil, some paper, and about 20 small things you can count — beans, stones, or bottle caps. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: say your answer out loud or type it, then tell me HOW you worked it out. In my class, the thinking matters as much as the answer! There are six steps. Here comes step one. Amina has 12 dates. Yusuf gives her 5 more. Which number should you start counting from — 12 or 5?

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are on Learn the Method. A method is a set of steps we follow to work out an answer. Our first method is Counting On to Add — adding by starting at the bigger number and hopping forward. By the end, you will be able to add two numbers up to 20 without counting everything from one. You will need a pencil, some paper, and about 20 small things you can count — beans, stones, or bottle caps are perfect. There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Take this sum — 12 + 5. Look at the two numbers and tell me which one is bigger. That bigger number is where we start counting. What do you think? 😊

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today we are on the Visual Models page. A visual model is just a picture that shows what the maths is doing. We will use a number line and some little objects so you can SEE adding and taking away, not just hear about them. By the end you will be able to show 12 add 5 and 16 take away 4 as hops, and split a number into two parts. What I expect from you: try each step yourself, say your answer out loud or type it, and tell me the number you land on. There are 5 steps. Here comes step 1. Get 20 small things you can count — beans, stones, buttons, or bottle caps. Then take paper and a pencil, and draw a long line. Write the numbers 0 to 20 along it, evenly spaced. A good number line has every number, in order, with the same gap between each one. Tell me when it is ready. Take your time — there's no rush.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today we are on the Worked Examples page. A worked example is a sum that shows you every step, like a teacher thinking out loud. We do this so you learn the way to get the answer, not just the answer. By the end you will be able to count on to add and count back to take away, up to 20. You will need a pencil, some paper, and about 20 small things you can count — beans, stones or bottle caps are perfect. We will do 4 steps together. Here comes step one. Step 1: our sum is 12 add 5. Do not count all your beans from one. Look at the two numbers, 12 and 5, and tell me which one is the BIGGER number. That bigger number is where we start. Tell me your answer, and I will wait. 🙂

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Guided Practice. This activity is where you try the sums yourself, one at a time. We do it so that adding and taking away to 20 becomes easy and quick for you. By the end, you will be able to count on to add and count back to take away, all the way to 20. You will need a pencil, paper, and about 20 small things to count — beans, stones, or bottle caps. There are 12 questions on your page. We will do them in small groups. I expect you to try each one first, tell me your answer, AND tell me how you counted. Saying how you counted is the most important part! Here comes question one. 10 add 4 equals what? Start at 10 and count on 4. Take your time — there's no rush.

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing the "Practise together" activity. 😊

Here is what it is: you pick one idea from Unit 13, make a model of it, explain it to someone at home, and then write your very own question. Why we do it: when you teach an idea to someone else, it sticks in your head much better. Mathematicians do this all the time! What you need: paper, a pencil, and about 20 small things you can count — beans, stones, buttons, or bottle caps. What I expect from you: try each step yourself, say your numbers out loud, and tell me when you are done so I can check. There are 4 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Choose ONE idea from this unit to work with. You can pick counting on to add, counting back to take away, or splitting a number into two parts. Which one do you choose?

games.label: Games
games.text:
Welcome to the Games page! 🎉

Here is what this is. These are quick maths games about adding and taking away numbers up to 20. Each game gives you four little questions with answers to choose from. We play them because playing makes your counting fast and strong, like practising kicking a ball. By the end, you will be able to count on and count back to 20 without stopping to think for long. What you need: your pencil, some paper, and about 20 small things you can count — beans, stones, or bottle caps. Your fingers work too! What I expect from you: pick an answer, and then tell me HOW you got it. The "how" matters more than the answer. Guessing is okay sometimes, but I will always ask you to show me your counting. We will do four rounds together. Here comes question one. Add by counting on: 12 add 5 equals what? Is it 16, 17, 18, or 15? Take your time — there's no rush.

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today we are doing Math Fluency. That means quick practice with adding and taking away up to 20. We do it so counting on and counting back become fast and easy for you, like tying your shoes. By the end you will be able to add and subtract up to 20 without counting everything from one. You will need a pencil, some paper, and about 20 small things you can count — beans, buttons, or bottle caps. There are 6 short questions. I will give you one at a time, and I will wait for your answer each time. Say your answer, and tell me how you got it. Here comes question one. 12 + 5 = ? Start at the bigger number and count on. Take your time — there's no rush.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Welcome to Solve Real Problems! On this page you get little stories from real life — dates in a bowl, mangoes at the market, people on a bus. Your job is to read the story, decide if it is an adding story or a take-away story, then count on or count back to find the answer. We do this because real maths lives in stories, not just in sums. By the end you will be able to hear a story and know which way to hop on the number line. What you need: a pencil, some paper, and about 20 small things you can count — beans, bottle caps or stones. Your grown-up can help you gather them. There are 6 stories. Here comes story one. Amina has 11 dates in a bowl at home. Her brother gives her 7 more dates. How many dates does she have now? First, don't tell me the total yet. Just tell me this: is this an adding story or a take-away story? And why do you think so?

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Welcome to Explain Your Thinking! 🌟

On this page you do not just give an answer. You say HOW you worked it out, in your own words. We do this because explaining helps the idea stick in your head. By the end, you will be able to tell me why we count on from the bigger number. You will need your voice and maybe some small things to count, like beans or bottle caps. There are 3 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Get ready with a real example. Take 12 beans in one pile and 5 beans in another pile. Then tell me: which pile is bigger? Just say the number.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Unit Challenge. Here is what it is. You will pick one big idea from Unit 13, make it into a model you can see, and then teach it to someone in your family. At the end you will write your very own maths question and solve it. Why do we do it? Because when you can show an idea and explain it out loud, it really sticks in your head. Teaching is the best kind of learning! What I expect from you: try each step, talk to me after each one, and use real things you can hold. Get ready a pencil, some paper, and about 20 small objects — dates, beans, stones or bottle caps. There are 4 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Choose ONE idea from this unit. You could choose counting on to add, counting back to take away, a number line, or splitting a number into two parts. Tell me which one you choose. Any of them is a good choice — just say it in your own words, like "I choose counting back."

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Welcome to Unit 14! I'm your teacher today. This unit is called Sorting and Organising Data. Data is a big word that just means information we collect about things. We are doing this overview first so you know what is coming, like looking at a map before a trip. By the end of this unit you will be able to sort things into groups, make a picture chart, and say which group has the most. What I expect from you: listen, think, and answer me in your own words. There are no wrong tries here — trying is the work. There are 4 steps. Here is step 1. Look around the room and find a small pile of things you could put into groups — maybe toys, socks, spoons, or crayons. Tell me what you found.

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. 🌟

This lesson is called Sorting and Organising Data. Data means information we collect about things. We will learn to put things into groups, then show them on a picture chart so we can see which group has the most. I would like you to have a pencil, some paper, and a few small things nearby — buttons, stones, crayons or toys. Talk out loud and tell me your answers. Good work here means you say the rule you used, and you count each group. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one! Step 1: Put about six small things in front of you. Now sort them by colour. That means put the same colours together in little piles. Tell me when you are done, and tell me how many piles you made.

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text: Welcome! This page is our Maths Words page. It holds the special words we use when we sort things and make charts. We learn these words so that when a question says "which has the most?" you know exactly what it wants. There are nine words. We will take them three at a time, so it stays easy. Here is what I expect from you: after each word, you say it back in your own words, and then make one sentence with it about your own home. Short sentences are perfect. You just need your voice, and maybe a pencil. Let's start with something small. Step 1 of 9. Our first word is data. Data means information we collect about things. Like when you count how many spoons are on the table, or ask your family their favourite fruit — those answers are data. Now you try: tell me some data you could collect at home. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Welcome! Today we are exploring sorting. Sorting means putting things into groups. We do it so we can count each group and see which has more. By the end, you will sort things by a rule, use a sorting circle, and read a picture chart. You just need your eyes, your brain, and your voice. A pencil is nice too. There are 6 little steps. Here comes step one. Step 1. Imagine a pile of stones on the mat. Some are white, some are black, some are brown. Our rule is colour. You pick up a white stone. Which group does it join?

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Welcome to Visual Models! 🌟

On this page we look at little pictures that show how we sort things and show data. Data just means information we collect about things. We do this so that when you see a sorting circle or a pictogram later, your brain says "oh, I know this one!"

There are six models on the page. I will take you through them one at a time. You will need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil. Here is what I expect from you: look at each model, then tell me in your own words what you see. Short answers are perfect. Step 1: Find the first model, called Sorting by One Attribute. It shows things put into groups. Look at it, then tell me: what rule do you think was used to put the things in groups — colour, size, or shape?

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Learn the Method. A method is just a recipe — the steps we follow to do a job. On this page we learn the steps for sorting things into groups and for reading picture charts. By the end, you will be able to sort objects by one rule and count each group. You need a pencil, some paper, and a small pile of things from home — buttons, spoons, socks or toys. Here is what I expect from you: try each step out loud or with your hands, and tell me what you got. Short answers are perfect. Our first method has 3 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Choose one rule to sort by. A rule can be colour, or size, or shape. Look at your pile of things and tell me: which rule will you use? 😊

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today we are on the Worked Examples page. A worked example is a maths problem with the answer already shown, step by step, like watching me cook before you cook. We do this so you can see HOW to think, not just what the answer is. By the end you will be able to sort things into groups, count a row of pictures, and say which group has the most. You need your eyes, your counting finger, and maybe a pencil and paper. There are 4 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1. Here is the example: There are 3 white stones, 2 black stones and 1 brown stone. We sort them by colour. I want you to tell me one thing: how many groups do we make? Say the number, and tell me why.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Welcome! This is our Guided Practice for Unit 14. Guided Practice means we do sorting questions together, one at a time. We are doing it so you get good at putting things into groups and reading picture charts. By the end, you will be able to sort things by a rule and say which group has the most. You just need your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a pencil and paper. Here is what I expect from you: give me your answer, then tell me HOW you worked it out. Mathematicians think slowly on purpose, so take your time. There are 12 little questions. Here comes question one. Imagine you have some stones: 3 white ones, 2 black ones, and 1 brown one. Our rule is colour. If you sort them by colour, how many groups do you make?

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing the "Practise together" activity. In this activity you pick one big idea from Unit 14 — sorting, a sorting circle, a pictogram or a block graph — and you make it real with your own things at home. We do this because sorting and charts make much more sense when you touch them and build them, not just look at them. By the end, you will be able to sort things by a rule, show them in a chart, and explain your chart out loud. You will need paper, a pencil, and some small things from home, like buttons, spoons, socks or toys. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 4 steps. Here is step 1. Step 1: Choose ONE idea to practise. You can pick sorting by colour, a sorting circle, or a pictogram. What I expect: just tell me which one you choose, and say it in a full sentence, like "I choose sorting by colour."

Which one do you choose?

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text:
Welcome to Math Fluency! 🌟

This is our quick practice page. I will ask you short questions about sorting things into groups and reading picture charts. We do this so your brain gets fast and sure — like tying your shoes without thinking. There are 12 questions, in 3 rounds of 4. Here is what I expect from you: say your answer, then tell me how you got it. Take your time — there's no rush. Here comes question one. Round 1, question 1:
You sort beads by colour. There are 4 red beads and 2 blue beads. How many groups do you make?

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the Unit 14 games. Each game gives you four little questions about sorting and charts. Sorting means putting things into groups. By the end, you will be quicker at spotting which group something belongs to, and at reading pictures in a chart. What I expect from you: read each question slowly, choose your answer yourself, and tell me why you picked it. Take your time — there's no rush. There are three steps. Here comes step one. Step one: look at your screen and find the first game, called "Quick Match: Data". Tap it to open it. Tell me when it opens, and read me the first question. 🙂

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Welcome! This page is called Solve Real Problems. Here we use sorting and counting to answer questions from real life — like fruit in a bowl, or toys on the floor. We do this because charts and groups help us see which group has more and which has less. I will give you one problem at a time. I want you to tell me your answer AND how you worked it out. Counting on your fingers is allowed! 😊

You need your eyes, your fingers, and maybe a pencil. There are 6 problems. Here comes question one. At home, you sort the fruit bowl. There are 4 mangoes, 1 banana, and 2 oranges. Which fruit has the least? Take your time — there's no rush.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Welcome! This page is called Explain Your Thinking. Here you do not just say the answer. You say HOW you got it. Telling your thinking out loud is what real mathematicians do — it helps the idea stick in your head. We have three little thinking tasks. All you need is your eyes, your counting finger, and your voice. You can type your answer, or say it to your grown-up. What I expect from you: not one word, but a small sentence with a "because" in it. Like "There are 4 because I counted them one by one."

Here comes step one. Look at this row of camel pictures:

Camel: 🐫🐫🐫

Tell me how you would count them, and what the count tells you.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Welcome to your Unit Challenge! 🌟

This is where you show off everything you learned about sorting and charts. You will make your own little model of one idea from this unit, then teach it to someone in your family. By the end, you will be the one explaining maths — that is a big deal! You need paper, a pencil, and some small things from home you can sort. Stones, buttons, spoons, socks or toys all work well. There are four steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Choose ONE idea from this unit for your challenge. You could choose sorting by a rule, the sorting circle, the sorting box, or making a pictogram. What I expect: just tell me which one you pick, and say it in your own words — like "I pick sorting, that means putting things into groups."

Which one do you choose?

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Unit Overview for Unit 15: Time. This page is our map. It shows what we will learn: the seven days of the week, the twelve months of the year, the words yesterday, today and tomorrow, and how to read a clock. We look at the map first so you know where we are going. By the end of this activity you will be able to tell me the big ideas of this unit in your own words. You will need your voice and your fingers for counting. I expect you to try an answer every time I ask, even if you are not sure. Trying is the whole job. There are 4 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: The days of the week. Say all seven days out loud, starting with Monday. Hold up one finger for each day. Then type them here for me. A good answer has seven days, in order, with none missed. 🙂

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. 😊

This lesson is called Time (2): Days, Months and Clocks. We will learn the seven days of the week, the twelve months of the year, and how to read a clock. By the end, you will be able to say what day comes next and read times like 3 o'clock and half past 3. All you need is your voice, and a pencil and paper if you like. There are six small steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: The days of the week. Say these out loud with me, and clap once for each one: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. That is seven days, and they always come in the same order. Now you try. Say all seven days out loud, then type them here for me. A good answer has all seven, in order, with none missed out.

words.label: Math Words & Symbols
words.text:
Welcome! This page is our Maths Words page for Unit 15. It holds the special time words we use, like week, o'clock and hour hand. We learn them so that when I say "the hour hand", you know exactly what I mean. We will do this in 4 steps. We will learn three words at a time, then check them all at the end. You just need your voice and your thinking brain! 🙂

Step 1: Our first three words are week, yesterday and tomorrow. A week is a group of seven days. Yesterday is the day before today. Tomorrow is the day after today. Now you try one. Tell me: how many days are in a week?

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models page. 🕐

Visual models are pictures that help us see time. On this page there are six of them: a days wheel, a yesterday-today-tomorrow line, a months circle, and clocks for o'clock and half past. We do this because pictures make time easy to remember. By the end, you will read a clock and say the days in order all by yourself. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. There are six steps. Step 1: Look at the first model, the Days of the Week wheel. Say all seven days out loud, starting at Monday. Clap once for each day. Then type them here for me.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Welcome! Today we are on the Explore the Concept page for Time. This activity is a set of six little thinking questions. Each one shows you one time idea — days, months, and clocks — and asks you to work it out yourself. We do it this way because you remember much better when YOU find the answer than when I tell you. By the end, you will be able to say the days and months in order, use yesterday and tomorrow, and read o'clock and half past on a clock. You need your voice, and maybe a pencil. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. What I expect from you: try each answer out loud or type it, even if you are not sure. Guessing bravely is allowed. Mistakes are how we learn. There are six steps. Here comes step one! Step 1: The Days of the Week. The week is like a wheel. It turns round and round: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday... and then it starts again. My question for you: What day comes right after Sunday?

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. 🙂

This page is called Learn the Method. A method is just a way of doing something, step by step. On this page we learn six methods for time: saying the days, saying yesterday and tomorrow, saying the months, reading o'clock, reading half past, and putting your day in order. We do this so you can look at any clock and any calendar and know what it says. By the end, you will be able to do these on your own. What I expect from you: say the words out loud, not just in your head. Have seven small things ready, like stones, buttons or crayons. Take your time — there's no rush. Let's start with Method 1: the days of the week. It has three little steps. Step 1: Put your seven stones in a line in front of you. Tell me when they are ready.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Worked Examples. A worked example is a question with the thinking shown, step by step. We do them so you can see HOW to think, not just what the answer is. By the end, you will be able to say the days and months in order, and read a clock. Here is what I expect from you: try each one yourself first, out loud or in your head, then tell me your answer. Wrong answers are welcome — mistakes are how we learn. You will need your voice, and a pencil if you like. There are 12 examples on this page. We will take them one at a time. Step 1. Say the days of the week in order, starting from Monday. Clap once for each day. Then type them here for me.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Guided Practice. Guided Practice means we do time questions together, one at a time. We are doing it so you get quick and sure with days, months and clocks. By the end, you will be able to say the days in order, find yesterday and tomorrow, and read a clock. You will need your voice, and a pencil if you like writing. Here is what I expect from you: try each one yourself first, then tell me your answer. If you get stuck, say "stuck" and I will give you a small hint. 😊

There are 12 little steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Say the days of the week in order, starting from Monday. Count them on your fingers as you go. Type them out for me.

activities.label: Activities
activities.text:
Lovely! Let's do this activity together. 😊

This activity is called Practise Together. You will pick one time idea from this unit, make it with your hands, and teach it to someone in your family. We do it because when you teach something, it sticks in your brain for good. By the end you will have your very own time model and one question you made yourself. You will need paper, a pencil, and maybe some small things from home like stones, buttons, or a paper plate. There are four steps, and I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Choose your idea. Pick ONE of these:
the days of the week
the months of the year
a clock showing o'clock and half past

Which one do you want to make? Tell me your choice.

fluency.label: Math Fluency
fluency.text: Welcome to Math Fluency! This is our quick-thinking game about time. I will ask you short questions about days, months and clocks. You answer as fast as you can, but taking your time is fine too. By the end, the days and months will pop into your head without hard thinking. You just need your voice and your fingers for counting. There are 12 questions, in 3 rounds of 4. What I expect from you: give me your answer, and if I ask "how did you know?", tell me the little step you did in your head. Guessing is okay — we fix it together. Here comes question one. What day comes after Monday?

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Games page in Unit 15, Time. These games are quick little challenges about days, months and clocks. We play them so the days, months and clock hands stay in your head — like a song you can sing without thinking. By the end you will be quicker at saying what comes next, and at reading o'clock and half past. Here is what I expect from you: try your own answer first, even if you are not sure. A guess with thinking behind it is great. If you get stuck, say "stuck" and I will give you a small hint — never the answer. There are 4 steps. Ready? Here comes step one. Step 1: Look at the games on your screen and find the first one, called Quick Match: Week. Tap it to open it. Tell me when it is open. 😊

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Welcome to Solve Real Problems! 🌟

On this page you use time words in real stories about real people. Each little story has a question about days or months. We do this because time is not just for the clock on the wall — you use days and months every day, like knowing when Jummah is. By the end you will read a story, find the time word in it, and answer with the right day or month. You need your eyes, your ears, and your fingers for counting the days. There are 6 stories in all. Here comes question one. At home, Amina helps her mother cook a special family meal every Friday. What day of the week is the special meal? Read the story twice. The day is hiding right there in the words — find it and tell me. Take your time.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Explain Your Thinking". In this activity you do not just say the answer — you say HOW you know. That is a big grown-up maths skill. By the end, you will be able to explain a day answer in your own words, using words like today, yesterday and tomorrow. You need your voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby to listen. We will do 3 steps, one at a time. Here comes step one. Step 1. Say the seven days of the week out loud, in order, starting at Monday. Clap once for each day. I am looking for all seven days, in the right order, with none missed and none said twice. Tell me when you have done it. 😊
